It is the department's established policy to move park superintendents from one park to another at intervals of approximately five years. This ensures that the superintendents will gain wide experience and will have the opportunity to develop their abilities to the fullest extent. It also ensures that a new viewpoint will be brought to the problems of administering each park at reasonable intervals, and at the same time helps to achieve uniformity in the handling of administrative details which are common to all parks.

May I
ask the Prime Minister a second question? Is the government contemplating either the abandonment or modification of the so-called policy of single station coverage with respect to television, that is to say the policy of local monopoly of television in Canada?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The question is not one to which a categorical yes or no can be given. The policy has never been that there would be, for all time, only one station in each locality. The whole matter is under constant consideration, and the question as to when it will be deemed proper to declare that applications for duplication of service will be entertained is part of that consideration. It may very well be that no decision would be arrived at before the appointment of the commission to which the hon. member referred in his previous question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would point out to the committee that the item is found at page 31 of the main estimates, and the details appear at page 246. Shall the resolution carry?

speakeroldname: Hon. Milton F. Gregg (Minister of Labour):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am never quite sure whether hon. members would prefer to have me make way at once for members to discuss my estimates, on the one hand, or whether they would like a short statement concerning special items of interest, on the other. I am prepared today to follow either course. It is only in the hope that it might expedite the passing of my estimates that, unless someone objects, I shall choose the latter.
The main estimates of the department and the unemployment insurance commission for 1955-56 total $69,542,295, as compared with $72,874,271, including supplementaries, for 1954-55, or a reduction of $3,331,976. This is accounted for partly by a reduction in the estimate of the government's contribution to the unemployment insurance fund, and partly by the fact that the Department of Public Works has been given the responsibility for building, maintenance and rental of premises for the unemployment insurance commission, costs which before were largely borne by the commission.
There is also a reduction in the item for vocational training capital expenditures, because our commitment under the agreement with the provinces has been fulfilled. There is a reduction in the services covering the movement of immigrants for work on farms and to fill other unsatisfied labour demands. These are the main items that cause the reduction in the vote; there are, of course, others. There are some slight increases in certain items which I shall refer to when I come to them.

On the question of staff, there is a slight change from last year; a reduction of 12 positions in the Department of Labour, partly owing to curtailment in certain fields of operation. But it will be noted from page 262 of the blue book on estimates that there is an increase of 304 in the establishment for the unemployment insurance commission. The increase is caused by the fixing of larger continuing establishments for many offices, owing to the increase in work load resulting from an increase in benefit claims.
At this point I should like to express my recognition and appreciation of the excellent work which the staff of both the Department of Labour and the unemployment insurance commission have continued to render. I think they are deserving of high praise, and are a credit to our public service.
Now, to comment briefly on some of the activities for which these estimates provide, let me deal first with the annuities branch, item 175. There are at present 350,000 persons covered by Canadian government annuities. Approximately 68,000 of these people are actually in receipt of their annuities, to a total of $32 million a year. Annual premium income for the year ended March 31, 1955, was about $66 million, which is an increase of around $2 million over the previous year. The annuities fund, as at March 31, 1955, amounted to $864,543,038. During the past year there has been an increase in sales, particularly of individual contracts, which show an increase of 18 per cent over the previous year.
I need not emphasize the national importance of the work performed by the industrial relations branch, which covers conciliation services, administration of legislation governing wages and working conditions on government contracts, the development of labour-management co-operation, and many other lesser activities. These are in vote 176.
The moneys voted last year for these purposes were well spent. There were 80 industrial disputes dealt with during the past fiscal year. In 48 of these 80 cases, settlements of the disputes were secured by conciliation officers. In 25 cases conciliation boards were established during the year, and reports were also received from five conciliation boards established during the previous fiscal year. Settlements were made on the basis of the boards' recommendations in nine of these disputes. There were six disputes in the hands of conciliation officers, and 18 disputes referred to conciliation boards which were still being dealt with at the end of the fiscal year.
Aside from the cases I have mentioned as still pending, out of 80 industrial disputes
Supply-Labour
all except three were settled during the year. In two of the three legal strikes occurred, and the third was settled by arbitration.
This industrial relations branch is also responsible for the administration of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. This involves the functions of the Canada labour relations board and the administration of the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act. These services are covered in the estimates under items 177 and 178.
The Canada labour relations board dealt with 65 applications for the certification of bargaining agents during the fiscal year, of which 53 applications originated during that period. Of the 65 applications mentioned, 34 were granted, 5 were rejected, 12 were withdrawn, and 14 were still being investigated on March 31. In disposing of these cases the board ordered 14 representation votes, which were conducted by officers of the department.
Last year I mentioned particularly the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act, which was then a new piece of legislation, and stated that a broader program of educational activity was planned. As part of this program two series of radio talks, one in English and one in French, were arranged during the fiscal year just ended. Other publicity measures included a distribution of pamphlets and posters describing the provisions of the act. Between July 1, 1953, when the act came into effect, and March 31, 1955, a total of 11 complaints were made under the act. Of the 8 made during the past fiscal year, 6 were settled either by direct investigation and conciliation or by correspondence, and 2 were under investigation as of March 31, 1955.
It is proposed to continue the farm labour program which has been continuously in operation since world war II, and the funds required are shown in vote 181. Under this program agreements are entered into with the provinces to provide for the sharing of the costs of organized movements of farm workers to meet seasonal demands in different areas. The provinces have asked that the program be continued, and after consultation with them it has been decided that a program sufficient to take care of this year's needs can be carried on with a reduction of $75,000 from the amount provided last year.
In addition to the farm labour program, which is designed to make the most effective use of the farm labour force within Canada, it has been necessary from time to time to bring immigrant farm workers to Canada in organized groups. Similar organized group movements have been necessary to meet

Supply-Labour
labour demands in several other basic industries. Funds for services connected therewith are provided under item 190. Last year an amount of $325,000 was included for transportation costs. This year any transportation required for these movements will be provided from funds voted to the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. For this reason, and because the movements this year are expected to be somewhat smaller, the amount provided in vote 190 represents a reduction of $411,385 from the amount provided in 1954-55.
Last year when the estimates were before the committee the director of the new women's bureau had just been appointed. I am now happy to say that the new branch has now been staffed and in operation for the past nine months. The director is Miss Marion V. Royce, a lady who is proving very well qualified by training and experience to give proper attention to the problems of women in employment. Ground work has already been laid for a survey to be undertaken of married women in employment. In view of the economic and social implications of the growing participation of married women in the labour force, the bureau regards this as an important area of investigation. It is also planned to undertake two additional projects of research during the coming year; a study of the occupational distribution of women in Canada, and in the field of women's earnings. The administrative costs of the branch are provided for under item 182.
I mentioned last year the initial steps that had been taken to establish a comprehensive plan for the rehabilitation of Canada's disabled. In co-operation with the Department of National Health and Welfare and the Department of Veterans Affairs, and in close consultation with the national advisory committee on rehabilitation, the provinces and voluntary agencies, these plans are going forward.
Eight of the provinces are now making use of the agreement whereby a maximum contribution of $15,000 a year is made through my department, on a matching basis, toward the salaries and expenses of a provincial co-ordinator and his staff, and toward the cost of supplying certain rehabilitation services not otherwise provided for. This is shown under item 183. The province of Ontario, in addition, has appointed a director of rehabilitation services, and discussions are going forward with that province regarding the possible signing of this agreement.
During the past year eight provinces have appointed provincial co-ordinators of rehabilitation. In these provinces improved

facilities for rehabilitating the disabled through the Vocational Training Co-ordination Act are now being utilized, and my colleague the Minister of National Health and Welfare will be reporting to you that in nine of the provinces the new medical rehabilitation grant is being used to expand facilities and train the staff necessary for the medical side of the program.
While the program is new and much has yet to be done, a good start has been made. I am impressed by the calibre of the men selected by the provinces to head up this program, and you will be glad, as I am, to know that as experience is gained, more and more of our disabled will be equipped to live more useful and satisfying lives.
The vocational training program under the Vocational Training Co-ordination Act, which is provided for under items 184, 185 and 186, accounts for approximately $4,500,000 of our total estimates for the year, so I think it is deserving of special mention although there is little change in the program from last year. Hon. members are aware that this program is a joint undertaking with the provinces, and with few exceptions the projects are based on a dollar for dollar contribution.
I mentioned earlier in my remarks that our commitments under agreement with the provinces for capital expenditures on vocational schools had been fulfilled. I referred to the $10,300,000 federal allotment which had been made since 1945 to be spent over a period of years on buildings and equipment to assist the provinces to enlarge and improve their vocational school facilities. At the close of the fiscal year 1954-55 federal payments under this program amounted to $9,722,374. The small amount which is requested under vote 186 is intended to provide for a few delayed claims from the provinces, and is in fact a revote.
Other vocational training programs which have been in effect for some years and which will be continued in 1955-56 include the training of apprentices, for which there is an annual expenditure of approximately $1 million; youth training, training of unemployed workers, foremanship and supervisory training, training of workers for defence industries, training of disabled persons, training of persons for the armed forces, etc. The detailed money provision for these various projects appears on page 255 of the blue book.
Mr. Chairman, I am not attempting here to report on all the services which come under the Department of Labour. If I were doing so, of course, I would make special mention of the work of our economics and

research branch, government employees compensation branch-on which there is legislation before the house-and also the publication of the Labour Gazette, which attempts to present factual information on labour matters of special interest from month to month.

Before the minister goes on, I do not want to break into his argument but he gave a reply today to a question I asked regarding vocational training. He stated in that reply:
The vocational schools assistance agreements entered into by the government of Canada with the provinces under the authority of the Vocational Training Co-ordination Act provided federal government financial assistance to the provinces for the development and carrying on of vocational training at a secondary school level.
Have all the provinces entered into agreements for the next year, so the same provision will be made as has been made in the past 10 years?

Mr. Chairman, I shall be prepared to discuss this item in more detail when we come to it; but to answer my hon. friend's question, as he knows the Vocational Training Co-ordination Act has a large number of schedules. There is "M" for unemployed persons, there is "R" for disabled persons, and so on. All the provinces have now either entered into an agreement for this year on the same basis as last year or are in process of doing so.
I turn now, Mr. Chairman, to the estimates of the unemployment insurance commission. Since there is legislation concerning the act before the house I am not going into it as fully as I did with regard to the department. There are three votes, one for the administration of the act, one for the contribution of the government to the fund, and one for the transfer of unemployed workers to areas where jobs are available.
The vote for administration shows a decrease over last year of $1,014,342. During the fiscal year 1954-55 an agreement was reached with the Department of Public Works by which in their estimates they would provide the necessary funds for looking after the rental of office accommodation, necessary alterations in offices and the providing of office furniture for the unemployment insurance commission.
During the years the commission has been in existence the services of the trained employees of the Department of Public Works were largely utilized for these purposes, but the funds were always voted by the unemployment insurance commission. The decrease accomplished in this manner is offset to some 50433-247
Supply-Labour
extent by a careful review that was made during the year of the work load in all the offices, which resulted in a small increase in the basic fixed establishment for regular positions. As you will observe, they were increased from 7,406 to 7,710. With the increase in the basic fixed establishments for the various offices it has been determined that the need for casual help during periods of seasonal unemployment, such as the winter months, will not be as great and a lesser amount has been provided for this purpose for the fiscal year 1955-56.
During the 12-month period from April 1, 1954 to March 31, 1955, a total of $257,628,602 was paid out in benefits, and the number of beneficiaries was approximately 1,001,000. Total contributions were $190,632,050, with the government contributing $31,771,740 of this amount. On March 31, 1955, the balance in the unemployment insurance fund was $840,692,317, a decrease of $40,581,817 over the balance on March 31, 1954. This decrease in the fund was due to the increased claim load during the period.
The most important function of the commission, of course, is the operation of the employment service. The value of this work cannot be overemphasized. During the last fiscal year 842,993 placements were made by our national employment service through its various offices across Canada.
The item for the transfer of labour also shows a decrease of $100,000. This item is designed to assist in the transfer of unemployed Canadian workers to places where employment is available. Expenditures made are recovered where possible from employers who are willing to pay the transportation cost of these transfers, and to that extent provide a revolving fund of working capital to aid in the movement of workers to jobs. Where such refunds cannot be assured, and where the minister finds that conditions in an area are such as to warrant such action, he may use this vote to assist unemployed workers in meeting the cost of moving to jobs elsewhere. The amount provided for the fiscal year 1954-55 was not required to the extent at first anticipated, owing to arrangements made with employers to refund the cost of transporting employees who were available for work in new localities.
That, Mr. Chairman, concludes my introductory remarks.

Mr. Chairman, the remarks the minister has made will probably help clear up some of the points on which we would undoubtedly have asked questions. However, there are still some things that are not particularly clear. I refer particularly to

Supply-Labour
the government's contribution to the unemployment insurance fund. I think we shall want more explicit information on that matter.
The reason I had not intended to go into the matter of unemployment insurance at this time is that, as the committee knows, the standing committee on industrial relations is even now sitting and considering amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act. There will therefore foe plenty of opportunity, I take it, for the committee to consider the various clauses of the new act and the administration of the old one, and also to ask such questions as we may wish at that time.
I was interested to hear the minister's report on the administration of the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act, and in particular to learn of the few complaints which had been received by the department. I think this is a point we should all consider. I recall that when we had before us the bill which became the act, speeches were made which sought to disparage the necessity for this type of legislation on the ground that in the various provinces in which it had been put into effect there had been so few complaints that is was thought the enactment of such legislation was scarcely necessary.
However, I like to take the other view and think that Canadians, generally speaking, are law-abiding people. When legislation is brought down the average Canadian reacts to it in a law-abiding manner, even if heretofore he has had different views and has acted in a manner different from the requirements of the act. He now pulls in his horns a bit and says, "After all, this is the law and I must abide by the law." I believe that is why, once legislation of this sort is enacted, we have so few complaints.
I am sure the minister will agree with me that even where we have complaints, a great many of them are readily settled by bringing the two parties together, or sometimes merely by a telephone call to the employer who had not realized that he had offended. Likewise, the complainant sometimes is at fault and when it is brought to the attention of that person he or she will readily admit that possibly he or she has imagined some of the things about which complaints were made. I know this has been the case in some instances, and I am sure it is the case with regard to many of the instances which come to the attention of the department by reason of the administration of this act.
This is a rather momentous year, Mr. Chairman, in labour matters in Canada. We are told that it will not be long now until two

major labour congresses in this country join in one large organization. I am sure that is a step we all welcome. I think it is not so much a matter of joining as it is a matter of admitting to themselves that, after all, they have the same objectives and must operate together under one head.
However, this amalgamation of interests in itself presents problems to the government, just as it will undoubtedly present problems to the two congresses themselves and to their local affiliates. I think this would be an appropriate time to draw attention to the fact that the government has not yet got down to a review of our labour laws. We in this party urged such action as long ago as the special session which was held in 1950, at the time the whole country was much upset over the strike of the railway workers. At that time we took particular exception to the institution of compulsory arbitration.
I should like, Mr. Speaker, for the sake of the record to quote briefly some of the comments which were made during the debate that took place on the bill brought down by the government at that time in an effort to form a basis for the settlement of that strike. Hon. members of this house who were here then, and others who are here now and who must have followed the deliberations of parliament on those very contentious matters, will recall that the clause in that bill to which we took particular exception was the clause which instituted a type of compulsory arbitration. Speaking on that occasion the Leader of the Opposition had this to say in part, and I quote from page 26 of Hansard for August 30, 1950:
Section 5 definitely and without any reservation provides tor compulsory arbitration.
Then he went on:
But compulsory arbitration, which is a principle that has not been regarded as acceptable in labour legislation in this country, is not something which, it seems to me, should be suddenly introduced in dealing with an emergency of this kind.
That, Mr. Chairman, has been one of our difficulties right along, that we wait until an urgent situation is upon us and then all of a sudden we try to solve it by some means or other that presents itself to us, without taking into consideration the long-term view.
On that same day the Leader of the Opposition had this to say:
Compulsory arbitration! That is a moderate term. I do not believe that any legislative body in this country, federal or provincial, would ever in its cool and calm senses consider for a moment the introduction of compulsory arbitration of this kind with no definition of the terms under which it was to be carried out.

Later that same day, after an amendment had been introduced, I find these words at page 61 of Hansard:
Over the years there has been free collective bargaining between the representatives of management and the workers in our great railway organizations. It is highly desirable that the principle of free collective bargaining be retained.
I quote now from page 72 of Hansard for the same day, when the Leader of the Opposition said:
The amendment now before us is simply a further attempt to carry new principles into legislation which at some future date may operate as a precedent, and those who find that being done will regard it as very unsatisfactory indeed. This section neither assures to the Canadian public the continued operation of the railroads in the months and years ahead, nor does it assure the workers the basic right of collective bargaining_
Then I skip a couple of sentences, and he went on:
I wish to make it quite clear that I regard it as something that is not only unsatisfactory to those directly affected by the limitation imposed by this section on the long established principle of collective bargaining; it is also unsatisfactory to the people of Canada because the bill offers no assurance that this will not happen again. It offers to the workers none of the assurances that their rights are going to be protected in the years ahead.
Then, Mr. Chairman, I should like to quote one short sentence from my own remarks on that same date, which will be found on page 75. I said in part:
I cannot see how those in the house, regardless of the party leadership they follow, who in their hearts believe in a system of free enterprise, to which we give unlimited lip service, can vote for a section like this which disrupts the management-worker relationships which have been built up in this country over a period of 50 years.
I have quoted those few short sections_________
and I could have quoted at much greater length, but it is not my desire at this time to delay the committee-in order to place on the record a few excerpts which will show the stand we in this party took at that time. We then asked for a review of Canadian labour legislation. We had some reason to expect that such a review might be undertaken. We asked the government to bring together the representatives of labour, management, and its own officials to consider a revision of the labour code. The government failed to act and now, some five years later, almost nothing has been done in this direction. Here we see another example, Mr. Chairman, of government stagnation in matters of national importance.
A couple of years ago in the industrial relations committee we were assured by the minister that the department was at work on a revision of the labour code. Last year I asked again when we could expect some
Supply-Labour
action. We have had no intimation whatever to date that such a revision will be forthcoming or even, I might add, any indication that the department is actually working on it, other than the hints which have been thrown out from time to time, none of them, I might say, very concrete.
In speaking of the necessity for a revision of the code, I should like to draw attention to the fact that conditions in this country have changed. The conditions under which workers find themselves employed today are far different from those under which they were employed a few years ago. The hours of work have been radically reduced; rates of pay have been changed, and as I mentioned before the amalgamation of the two great labour congresses is now imminent. Types of labour-management negotiations have evolved which were unheard of a few years ago. As a matter of fact, I might almost say that a very few years ago some of the labour negotiations which are taking place today would have been regarded as revolutionary. Today they are accepted.
Women have taken a much more important part in the production of goods and services in this country than formerly. In this regard I might point out that despite the fact that women have entered more and more into the labour market of Canada, there are still no women commissioners on either the civil service commission or the unemployment insurance commission. I know all the excuses which are given to this house for that lack. I cannot believe this situation could not be corrected, one way or another. However, the excuses still hold and not a new one has been added in the time I have been in this house.
There have been a few women appointed to committees, under certain circumstances, but those committees have been called only spasmodically or not at all. The reason given has been that there were subcommittees at work day by day and week by week. Eventually they will have a report to make about this particular situation or that, and then the committee will be called together to hear the report. In many instances the reports were not received and the main committees were not called together. Once again we see the old technique of appointing a committee and then smothering it.
Since I have already spoken of the participation of women in the labour force of this country, I should like to make a few remarks with reference to statements made by the minister when he mentioned what had happened to the women's bureau. He mentioned that the bureau has now had some nine

Supply-Labour
months of full operation. I look back at previous estimates and I find that in the estimates for 1953-54, in which the appropriation for the women's bureau was first set out, the amount set aside was $21,560, but that only $2,560 was spent during the year. Then last year, with the appointment of a director imminent, the minister budgeted for $24,090. Shortly after the estimates were passed the director was appointed and commenced her duties.
I am sure the first few weeks must have been confusing to her, and she must have had considerable difficulty in deciding just what required her attention first. In any event, when we come to the end of the year we find that instead of having spent $24,000, only $9,107 had been spent.
This year, with the bureau fully staffed and prepared to go ahead, has the appropriation been raised, or is there any provision for accelerating the activities of the bureau? No; the appropriation is approximately the same as last year, at $24,600. We would like to know what the bureau is doing and what are its plans. What are they going to do? The minister has said they have already undertaken a survey of married women who are working. I saw something in the newspaper to that effect over a month ago. About April 1 it was stated in the press that a questionnaire had been sent out to women's organizations.
I realize that women's organizations do tremendous work, and I am sure that from their ranks valuable information could be secured. But, after all, we have the women's division of the national employment service serving right across the country. These offices are well staffed with qualified personnel who undoubtedly could provide that information at what might be described as the professional level, rather than the hit-or-miss result which is bound to follow from a casual distribution of questionnaires sent out only to persons belonging to women's organizations. I do not approve of the method used in this instance. It is far from efficient, and I cannot see where it will produce the desired information.
I heard subsequently that this scheme had been dropped. Very soon thereafter I saw the article in the newspaper, so I presume this is a sort of off again on again procedure. The minister now says there is to be another survey in connection with occupational distribution of women workers, and a survey concerning their earnings. No doubt these surveys will produce interesting figures and information. But if they are to be undertaken in the same manner as the other survey I cannot see how we can hope to obtain
[Mrs. Fairclough.l
definite or conclusive results. Further, I do not see how it can be done on the very small amount of money appropriated for this bureau for the ensuing year. It is my impression that the bands of the bureau are tied, because I do not see how, with such a small appropriation, any plans could be carried out.
I would draw attention to the fact that we now have in Canada a labour force of 5,391,000, and that women comprise 22-33 per cent-almost 25 per cent-of that total labour force. In other words 1,204,000 women are gainfully employed in Canada. Their numbers have more than quadrupled in the last 10 years. Yet in the budget for the Department of Labour, amounting to something more than $6,500,000, the sum set aside for the women's bureau is only $24,600. I realize full well that the research facilities of the department are available to the bureau, arid that it would not be efficient for it to set up its own research facilities. I would hope the existing facilities are available to the director and her staff to the extent required. I must say, however, that the overall picture seems to show that the government attaches very little importance to women in employment.
The other big item of news on the labour front this year has been the extent to which unemployment reared its head during the past winter. We have had several debates in the house on the subject already. I heard on the radio first thing this morning that it was expected the presentation of the minister's estimates would precipitate another allout debate on unemployment. So far as I am concerned it is not my intention to dwell at length on that subject. I have already spoken on it on several occasions, and what I said still stands. I do not intend to take back a word of it.
However, in spite of debates we have had we have seen no action. In March, the last month for which figures are available, we saw the number of unemployed swell to an unheard of total of 632,900. The April figures should be due today or tomorrow. I dare say the minister has them on his desk right now, but we do not have them. The figures last month came out on the 19th, and several times the figures have come out on the 20th.
I have been wondering whether the date of bringing down the unemployment figures has anything to do with the discussion of these estimates today, rather than following the plan which had been proposed a few days ago by the leader of the house. We had expected the estimates of another department would be brought down first and that the estimates of the Department of Labour would follow. However, as time got short and

other debates in the house consumed a little more time than had been anticipated, perhaps the 20th of the month looked uncomfortably close, and it may be that the estimates of the Department of Labour are brought down now in the hope of disposing of them before it becomes necessary to release the number of unemployed persons for the month of April.
I can assure my hon. friend that consideration had nothing to do with the fact that we are discussing the estimates of this department today.
I am sure the minister would not expect me not to have my suspicions.
Quite a coincidence.

As the hon. member for Prince Albert says, it is quite a coincidence, in any event.
However, regardless of whether that was the reason for hurrying up these estimates- and I do not know the answer-we should ask ourselves what can be done. All through the debates on this subject one party or another has accused the members of other parties of having no consideration for the plight of the workers, of making no suggestions for their relief and offering no plans for the future.
Despite all those remarks, Mr. Chairman, I remember quite clearly hearing a number of good suggestions. Some of them even came from the supporters of the government itself; some came from members of this party; some came from other groups in this house. Surely all these suggestions taken together could not be discounted. Whether they would be workable is another matter. But I do not think any group in this house can point a finger at any other group and say you have no regard for the workers of this country, and you have made no constructive suggestions. I maintain that constructive suggestions have come from every quarter of the house, suggestions which have shown the concern which has been felt by hon. members over the situation in which we found ourselves last winter.
We might almost ask ourselves whether a debate on unemployment is just something that must be endured with the best possible grace by the government, after which it will resume its usual indifferent way. Ottawa, after all, like other capitals, has a rather synthetic quality, a quality which is very often present when a city is built as a capital. As we were told last evening at the dinner which was given by the federal district commission to the students who came here on the Rotary venture, Ottawa was built to house the
Supply-Labour
government. It has practically no industry but government. Not too long ago I came across an article in the Hamilton Spectator. In commenting on this state of affairs the writer had this to say, in part:
This is perhaps why its view of what is happening in the country at large is so often abstract and seems sometimes so downright unrealistic.
He was referring to Ottawa. He went on to say:
But a man standing in line at the employment office, without work . . . cannot be expected to look at things from a long, abstract perspective. His thinking cannot be expected to stretch to the nation's broad prospects for next year or the year after; it is bounded inescapably by his own immediate prospects for next week's food bill and next month's mortgage payment. He is simply up against a harsh and immediate reality.
The article then goes on to speak of the gap which exists between the point of view of the man in the unemployment queue and government officials who sit here in Ottawa, and it says:
Precisely because of the heartrending gap that exists .	.	. between things as they should be
(and one day will be again) and things as they are [DOT]-he and his fellows have every right to look to their prime minister and their government for a great deal more concrete help than they are today receiving.
With respect to concrete help, Mr. Chairman, I do not think for a moment the writer of this article was talking about handouts; he was not talking about the size of the unemployment insurance payments which those workers may receive if they qualify for benefits. He was talking about the broad picture of planning which it is undoubtedly this government's duty to undertake to ensure that this will not happen again.
As I said-and it was said last evening also-here in this building we are insulated against the reality of the day to day existence of some 15 million Canadians. We are unable to see the queues at the national employment offices across this land. We are insulated to a large extent from the distress of individuals. Their first thought is of their families. Here in this place an unreal atmosphere exists. It is the duty of every hon. member to dig beneath the superficialities, to come to grips with the task which is before them and to urge and urge until this government finally does take some steps to make sure that we shall not have a repetition of the situation which we endured last winter.
Several years ago a national advisory council on manpower was set up. Some very important people were appointed to that council, Mr. Chairman, and they met a few times. What happened to them I do not know. Rumours flow around these buildings like

Supply-Labour
water over a dam. I have no intention of being a rumourmonger. I know what must have activated some of these people. In an attempt to find out what happened, early in the session-as a matter of fact on March 3, at page 1675 of Hansard-I asked the minister whether the national advisory council had met this year at all. The minister replied that it had not yet met in this calendar year, but that it had met last year. The following day, having felt that he was in error, he proceeded to correct that statement and said, at page 1717 of Hansard:
This past year there have been meetings and activities of committees responsible to the council.
This bears out the remarks I made a few minutes ago about appointing councils and committees and then letting subcommittees do some of the work, but they never report to the main committee. Perhaps I had better quote the reply all over again, since I interpolated a remark, Mr. Chairman. The minister's remarks were these:
This past year there have been meetings and activities of committees responsible to the council she mentioned, but the last meeting of the full council itself was held on November 5, 1953.
The last meeting of the national advisory council on manpower was held a year and a half ago. Since that time we have had two bad winters of unemployment. It is quite true, Mr. Chairman, that the committee was probably not set up to deal with the problem of unemployment, but I submit that the ladies and gentlemen who sat on that committee were admirably suited1 to undertake just such a task. They also constitute the council, and it would have taken very little adjustment to have them change their pace and consider very seriously the problems which were before Canada. What better work have they to perform than to analyse the employment situation? Why should they not supply us with answers as to how we can create jobs? What figure is dangerous in the unemployment position? What industries in this country present the greatest problems? What plans should be made for the future development of Canada, population-wise and industrially? Where does the production of raw materials and their ultimate processing fit into the picture? How much food do we need? Can we produce all of it or what proportion of it? Can we produce it with the farm labour that is available in this country at the present time?
These are questions to which we must have the answers. It is not enough to ride the tide, be it full or ebb. Experiments are costly. The government is in urgent need of

detailed answers to these problems, answers which should be supplied before another winter confronts us.
As I said the other day in another debate, now is the time, in this spring of the year, when employment has started to pick up, when the edge is off the urgency, to be planning for next winter. Now is the time when the government should be undertaking these two main projects; one, the finding of answers to the problems which confront us in the field of unemployment, and two, a revision of the labour laws under which our people work today.

Mr. Chairman, I am going to try to be specific and as brief as possible. During this session we have gone into many aspects of the minister's department, and I do not see any point in discussing them again. Some of the things I might talk about at this time are being worked on, which is much more important than just talking about them. For example, the Unemployment Insurance Act is now before a committee, and we will have a chance to discuss that act in all its details.
Another matter I might go into at some length on the minister's estimates is the general condition of the coal mining industry in Nova Scotia and its relationship to unemployment. However, I am not going to do that at this time because a conference is commencing tomorrow in Halifax at which all the dignitaries of state will be present, including the Minister of Labour and representatives from the industry and the union. They will make a general examination of the industry and its future, and I hope will come up with some answers.
One of the matters to be considered is the proposal to close one of the major collieries in the Glace Bay area which will affect some 750 men. To that extent unemployment will be created which will have considerable effect on a large community. I mention that because I know the minister is going to be asked what he is going to do about those who will be added to the unemployment rolls if this colliery closure actually takes place. Personally I am in hopes that it will not.
This matter of anticipated further unemployment raises the question of vocational training. While the minister was making his statement I took a look at his estimates and got some idea why the Minister of Finance went into deficit budgeting. Apparently the Minister of Labour tried quite hard to help make up the anticipated deficit in the budget by cutting his estimates in a field which has much to do with the matter of unemployment. I was really surprised as I think

this is the very time when expenditures in that particular field should be increased.
If you look at the estimates you will find that the grants to provinces for vocational training purposes have been cut by $109,000, while the capital grants for the purpose of assisting in the providing of vocational schools have been cut by $651,450. I have said this a good many times in the house, but apparently not much attention is paid to what we say on this subject by the experts who do the figuring. I contend that if there is one field in which we are short in Canada it is the field of vocational training.
In justifying the cut in the estimates for vocational training the minister said they had met their commitments. They may have had commitments over the last five years under the agreements with the provinces, but that does not alter the fact that the need is greater today than it was when the agreements were first signed. The agreements have to be renewed, and the way to renew them is not by cutting out the money which was necessary in the past to maintain them.
I suggest seriously to the minister that this is something he will have to consider. We should stop and think of the great need in this country for vocational training of the boys and girls who are coming out of school. We have been very shortsighted in this whole field. Of the school population across Canada, about 40 per cent go through high school, and about 10 per cent of that 40 per cent get to university. Ninety per cent of our school population go into the ranks of the employed every year with nothing to sell. If these people are to become citizens able to make a maximum contribution they must be trained in trades or other lines of work for which they may be fitted.
These young people are citizens of Canada; some of them will be running this country in the future. Instead of recognizing the need for retraining in connection with industries where thousands and thousands of people are becoming unemployed every year, the minister's department is cutting the estimates. The needs for vocational training are very great today.
If the minister will stop and think for one moment he will realize that the greatest contributing factor to unemployment in Canada, and in the United States as far as that is concerned, is automation, the displacement of man by the machine. This word "automation" is being used to make it sound a little better, but all it means is that the employer is improving his machinery so he can get more production from fewer men.
Supply-Labour
Some day we will have to answer the question whether the machine is going to be the servant of man or man the servant of the machine.
Within the next few years we are going to find that automation will be putting more and more men on the street and we will be faced with the problem of retraining men for some other gainful occupation. Instead of doing that we are cutting down the very organization that is needed to train our men and women so they may make a contribution to the country. Instead of training people who might become displaced, we are going into reverse and practically cutting out these grants.
I was surprised and disappointed on looking at the estimates to see the extent to which vocational training was being disregarded at this time. I hope the minister will give further consideration to this matter and provide a vote in the supplementaries to offset the decreases in the estimates at this time. Before his estimates are finished I should like the minister to tell us why these reductions in the vocational training votes have been made. Were the provinces not interested in continuing them? Surely there must have been some correspondence with the provinces in regard to the agreements and their renewal. I should like to know what position was taken by the province from which I come, because one of the crying needs in that end of the country is a vocational training program, and this is particularly so in the face of automation.
The trouble in the mining industry in Nova Scotia today has been brought about largely by the introduction of new machinery. The Sydney steel plant was modernized, and a great deal of noise was made about the amount of money that went into that program. But this company was able to maintain the ratio of production it had in 1939 and through the war even though it got rid of 1,600 men in the process. They joined the ranks of the unemployed and moved to some other part of the country. They became displaced persons. If there had been some kind of retraining program they might have had an easier time finding other employment.
I have recommended to the minister many times something I think should be done. Whilst the advisory council on employment may serve a useful purpose, I do not think it is as practical as the kind of thing I think should be done. The men and women on the advisory council for employment are largely people who live in the city and have offices here, and they are out of touch with the industries as they exist today across the

Supply-Labour
country. I may have worked in the mining industry some years ago, but it has changed. The men who are on that council may have worked in an industry some years ago, but that industry has changed.
I have recommended to the minister a good many times the type of organization I think he should have. I believe what are known as industrial councils should be formed. I believe the minister should have a council for the automobile industry, for example, of men who work in and around that industry, so that when a proposal is made by the automobile employers to make a change-over in their equipment or machinery, before that happens he can sit down with men who are aware of what the impact of that particular change is going to mean in the community with regard to unemployment. Perhaps the industry and a representative from the union, from the men themselves who understand the situation, sitting around with the minister's advisers and counsellors, would be able to work out some formula that would offset the impact that particular change-over may have in the community.
In the way things are done today, where the employer is allowed to throw into the street two or three thousand people without any thought of their investment in the community, in my opinion he is accepting no social responsibility whatsoever. Through these industrial councils the minister's department, employer and employee can sit around and discuss the question. Then the government, which is expected to handle unemployment when it happens, will have some knowledge of what might be done, before it is all tangled up and just hopes something may happen to cure the ills of that particular industry.
You have an industrial council in the building trades. That industry has had one for years. It has sat down with the minister's officials from time to time and worked out formulas that have prevented difficulties and troubles in that industry over the years. If it is good for that industry, why is it not good for the automobile industry, for the textile industry, for the mining industry, for all these basic industries across the country in which there is dislocation because of automation? You would have firsthand information from people who are involved, from people who could give you much advice on the handling of the matter.
We can talk about unemployment as much as we like, but I do not think the government, in making cuts in the labour department estimates, is recognizing the situation at all. The trend is to reduce further the machinery that has been set up under the

minister's department in that particular field. I notice also that the administrative cost of the unemployment insurance commission is being cut at this time by $1,014,000.
Maybe we are getting more efficient.
I am not so sure of that. That will be answered in the future. You are just making this reduction. I do not think the burden of that commission is becoming less and less.

Perhaps my hon. friend would not mind my interrupting him. Most of that was due not to a cut in the services but rather to a change-over to the Department of Public Works of responsibility for the costs of buildings and maintenance of buildings, which we used to carry in our vote.

It might cost more in the long run. I am not going to argue the point, but I am just mentioning the fact that there is a cut. On the other hand, the hon. member for Vancouver South interjects that they are becoming more efficient. Maybe you are not paying enough wages to the people administering that act. I know the local people with whom I have contact from time to time, the managers of offices, the people who prepare claims and the insurance officers who adjudicate the claims, who are all very efficient, are very poorly paid considering their qualifications. If the minister had a million dollars to play around with, instead of cutting it off and giving it to the Minister of Finance to offset the deficit he thinks he is going to accumulate this year, it would be better if the minister used that money to increase the salaries of those who administer the act, and who do a very good job.
In that way the minister would be putting additional purchasing power in the hands of a certain section of the public, which might create jobs and offset unemployment in some industries. It is false economy to say simply, "We are not going to spend it this year; we do not need it", and let the Minister of Finance take it and maybe use it to pay the interest on the national debt to the banks. I cannot see it in that way. You should never let that amount of money get out of your hands. There are many places where you can use it in your own department.
I notice that this year there is a reduction of $100,000 in the vote for the transfer of labour. I do not think good judgment is shown in reducing that vote. If the maritime provinces continue the way they are going you may have many displaced persons on your hands in that part of the country

whom you may have to ship out to British Columbia or somewhere else to find employment. Instead of reducing that grant it should have at least remained as it was, until such time as the minister was convinced that we are going to get some stability in employment and are not going to have this shifting mobile labour reserve that is developing. We call it unemployment today; others used to call it something else. But with the number of unemployed there is today that transfer of labour vote should have remained at least as it was.
Seasonal unemployment was the main theme of a very long debate in this house. The minister said, "There is not much unemployment; what we have is seasonal, and there is not much to it". Well, he is going to fight that next year, and he is appropriating the huge sum of $25,000 to combat seasonal unemployment. In my judgment, the estimates of the minister's department this year are the most unrealistic I have seen for a long time. The reason may be that the Minister of Finance has made certain promises that he is going to balance the budget at all costs and he may be going to do it in this way. But I think it is the wrong way to do it.
I have suggested a few times in the house that part of the answer to many of the problems that plague us from time to time is the guaranteed annual wage. The last time I talked about that-and I am not going to go into details now-I suggested to the minister that there are two problems which confront this North American continent in the future. One of them is the question of automation. The fact is that the big industrialists who work on the resources of this country say when there is going to be employment or unemployment. It is a heritage of the system. The minister is not going to be in any position to cure that situation until he has some say in the regulation of those who work on the resources of this country.
Machinery is being improved all the time. As machinery is improved, you are automatically going to get more and more unemployment. Accepting that proposition as a fact- and it is a fact-the next question you must face is this. You are either going to have a guaranteed annual wage, under which the employees of a given industry are going to have an income the year round, or you are going to have to amend your Unemployment Insurance Act in order to cover everybody in the country. It is one thing or the other. The guaranteed annual wage is the preferable way of doing the thing because it will make industry contribute its fair share to the maintenance of their employees. You do not just take a horse and throw it out on the 50433-248

street. You do not just feed it when it is working for you. You must feed it all the
time.
I suggest that there is no one who today has a formula that he can say is workable or practicable. There are a great many people studying the matter. I myself have a number of ideas on it. However, I suggest that the minister should have an interdepartmental committee-and he has many qualified people in his department-who would sit down and make a detailed study of just what the guaranteed annual wage would mean in the basic industries across this country.
The automobile industry is one where you get three months of unemployment every time there is a swing-over in the model of a car. To some extent the mining industry in eastern Canada is seasonal because there is a slack period during the winter months when the St. Lawrence river is closed. The same thing is true in the steel industry. I believe the minister's department is perhaps the most capable organization in Canada to sit down and work out the details-and honestly to work at the thing-as to whether the guaranteed annual wage is a practical proposition or otherwise.
We in this country are beginning to meet problems that we are going to have to face up to. In the past we solved our unemployment problem and our automation problem by getting into a couple of wars. We do not want to do it in that way any more. As the international situation is today, it looks as though the hydrogen bomb and the atomic bomb have frightened people at least into the position that they are not going to have war. If they are not going to have war, let us not breed revolution by failing to provide at least food, clothing and shelter for people.
When you take a look at the conditions that are described from time to time in some of the booklets you pick up, which are put out by social workers who are obliged to work in the various communities and who see the impact of unemployment on family life in this country, you find that the situation is really staggering; it frightens you. I am not going to read from this publication. It is the Social Worker for April and it sets out the problem in Toronto from that particular angle. When you read it you say to yourself, "War is over, we hope. Now we face the realities of life as to whether we are going to produce for use or whether we are going to produce just in order to make millionaires". You are faced with that question. You have two contending orders of society. One is saying, "Your kind of society will not work", and we are saying, "It will work; cling to your freedom".

Supply-Labour
You cannot tell that kind of story to a fellow who is hungry, who is unemployed, who has a wife and four children whom they have taken from him because he is not able to feed them, who has been evicted from his home and has had his family broken up. You cannot tell that fellow that he has freedom, democracy and the right to work for a living. It just does not work. To him any change is welcome. We are getting all too many people across this country affected in that way. I know it is not a particularly easy thing for me to go back to my own part of the country and stand up and talk to a bunch of people who want to work, and who are hard-headed realists. All they want out of life is just a home and the right to look after their families. But if they are working two days a week, or are not able to do that, there is no use telling them to cling to the present system, that it is the best thing for them, because we have been telling them that now for 50 years. We must start to make some fundamental changes.
As I said before, I believe one of the changes we are going to have to make-and it is fairly well advanced in the United States today-is the establishment of the guaranteed minimum wage. I know about the fellow who wants to make $3 million a year for himself. He is not going to like that change. But it is not the taxes you pay or that kind of thing that matters; it is what you have left. These fellows will not be hurt too badly in the long run. Their homes will not be taken from them. They must be made to realize that the resources of this country belong to all of the people of this country.
Governments also must begin to realize that they are the custodians of the resources, that they hold them in trust and they must see that they are managed in the best interests of all of the people of this country. It is our responsibility to see that that is done. The government sets a good example in the matter of the guaranteed annual wage. All the permanent civil servants get it. Members of the House of Commons get it. All the managerial staff in industry get it. All the white-collar workers and the managers are paid whether the plant is working or not. The only people who are not paid are those who really produce in industry.
Another thing we are going to have to face up to is this matter of the age limit on getting into an industry today. If you are 40 years of age you are through working. For the benefit of the minister, inasmuch as he is going down to that conference in Halifax, I might say I am reliably informed that in that No. 1-B colliery that you are going to be asked something about, at least 60 per cent of the
[Mr. Gillis.l
men employed are over 40 years of age. When you are thrown out at that age you are not only unemployed; that is the death sentence, you are through living.
I believe the government could take a cue in that matter themselves, because under their civil service regulations they also enforce that kind of thing. They keep out of employment in the civil service men and women who have reached that age, and who merely want to go in to do office work. In my judgment they are more capable at that age than they are at 20. It would not be a bad idea if the government changed the regulations in that respect. There are a great many people they could employ but who cannot find employment because of that 40-year age limit in the civil service regulations.
Mr. Chairman, I have talked for longer than I had intended. As the minister's estimates are discussed item by item we shall likely have many more things to say to him. I shall just sit down and say no more now.

Mr. Chairman, it is not my intention to carry on a debate at this time. Some of the other hon. members have made that same statement but have carried on probably for their full 40 minutes anyway. I do not intend to do that. Most of my speeches are short.
Oh, oh.

They are as short as the occasion demands; let me put it that way. I think the Department of Labour of late has been doing something which has been long in coming, and which is going to result in a good deal of benefit to the working people of this country. I have in mind the rewriting of the Unemployment Insurance Act. Probably that is one of the most important things that will come before the House of Commons during this session.
We have been spending a great deal of time in the committee going over the Unemployment Insurance Act. I know we had quite a sitting on it this morning, and last week we had quite a go at it. We are going to have another go at it next week. Therefore I take it that it would not be appropriate to carry on any discussion on this occasion with regard to the Unemployment Insurance Act.
Some reference has been made to items in these estimates where there has been a decrease. The hon. member for Vancouver South a moment ago suggested that maybe that decrease was due to increased efficiency. I would hardly agree with that statement, because this department has to deal with

unemployment. If there has been that increase in efficiency, so the department is better able to handle that problem, then I would suggest to members on the other side of the house we should be having a decrease in unemployment rather than an increase. This year has shown a tremendous increase, and I do not think the prospects are any too good for next year. Certainly the fact that we have had such a tremendous increase in unemployment would not indicate that the department is being handled any more efficiently in that respect. I do not mean to imply that the minister is not capable, and I shall mention that later in the few remarks I have to make.
Some suggestions have been made concerning the expenditure on vocational training. I am quite concerned about vocational training. I feel that is something to which a good deal of attention should be paid, but I cannot see much sense in training people to do a job when, after they have completed their training, there is no job nor any prospect of one. I am not for a moment minimizing the fact that people should be trained. This is a period of specialization. Nearly all the industries across this country are demanding specialists because we are coming to that point in our industrial expansion when, as the member for Cape Breton South indicated, we are seeing greater production by machines. There is only one result that will follow from the increased use and increased efficiency of machines, and that will be increased unemployment. There cannot be any other answer.
I am not one who would suggest for a moment that we should decrease the use of machines in order to keep people at work. I do not think that is the purpose of civilization. I believe we should increase the use of the most technical machines to the point where, if the whole operation can be performed by pushing one button, so much the better. The hon. member for Cape Breton South seems to be concerned about that, at least to the point where he suggests something is going to have to be done. Of course it is. We in the Social Credit party have advocated for years that the solution is to take away the earning power of the machine and give it back to the people the machine displaced, so the people will be able to purchase the production of that machine. This philosophy is just beginning now to slowly seep into the minds of some, and as yet it has not permeated the minds of others.
Some may say, "Well, now, that is silly; you cannot do that." We are being forced to it gradually, but in the process of being forced 50433-2481
Supply-Labour
to it this year we have had over 632,000 unemployed. These people are not receiving enough to give them the standard of living to which they are entitled. We have family allowances, and what is that but a method of redistributing purchasing power? Certainly it is not done on a scientific basis. It is only a redistribution of the existing insufficient amount of purchasing power. Unemployment insurance is another means of distributing purchasing power to those people who are not actively employed in the production of goods and services. This principle is going to have to be continued. Another method is through the distribution of old age pensions.
This year we did increase the supplementary benefits under unemployment insurance for a limited period. As soon as that period is exhausted, then the worker is right back into the old rut. You have people with insufficient purchasing power who can buy only a limited amount of goods, and that reduces the amount of goods produced, so there is a still further decrease in the production of goods. Surely that is not such a deep secret that the members of this house or the officials of the minister's department cannot cope with it if they really get down to business.
It seems to me the minister's department is being placed in a very unfavourable position. He is being criticized for something over which he has no control. I believe we will have to consolidate two or three departments with the Department of Labour, such as trade and commerce and the department which deals with development of our natural resources.
And finance.

And finance, if you like, but particularly the three I mentioned. If we do not have developments in the Department of Trade and Commerce which result in extending our markets and our trade, then of course we should produce less goods for export. If we have no development of our natural resources to make available the goods and services this country can produce, then the Minister of Labour is being forced to look after the inefficiencies of the other two departments. The other departments say, "Here are these unemployed who are the result of the inefficiency of our departments; you look after them." He has no way of solving that problem. In fact, even if he were to go to the government-he can correct me if I am wrong-and ask for an increased appropriation to give these unemployed a decent standard of living, what would treasury board tell him? They would

Supply-Labour
say, you just cannot have any more money. How is the minister going to efficiently care for the ever-increasing number who become unemployed as a result of the inefficiency of other departments in the government over which he has no control.
Including finance.

It seems to me that when we are talking about the labour department it is directly connected with these other departments I have named. The other day I said I thought there was no minister who ever headed that department who was more sympathetic to the problems that are facing him than the present Minister of Labour.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Hear, hear.

I am not going to pat him on the back too much, because I think he should listen to what I have to say and then get after these other ministers who are really responsible for the unemployment problem. In this house we indicate by our actions and our speeches that the Minister of Labour is the one who is responsible for unemployment. That is not true. He may be responsible for keeping the unemployed, for maintaining them while they are unemployed, but that is all. He has said, and the government have said, that this unemployment is only a seasonal condition; after a few weeks the unemployed will be taken care of. That is not true. Even the Minister of Labour and the government have to recognize that this tremendous increase in unemployment that we are experiencing today is not seasonal. It is something that is going to stay with us for quite some time.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South indicated that in the past the solution to this problem has been the intervention of war. He indicated, further, that probably because of the H-bomb people were becoming fearful of the results of war, and the nations of the world were not going to war because of the fear of extermination. I am sure everybody would be pleased if that were true. If it is true we will not have war to come to our assistance and bolster up the old, outmoded, orthodox system that has always failed in cases of emergency. The only time it has ever come through is when we have had a major catastrophe such as war.
Making a good C.C.F. speech.
The socialists are having more trouble, where socialism is practised in any other part of the world.
They cannot get production.

My hon. friend says I am making a good socialist speech. God forbid! Even they themselves prosper from the fruits of private enterprise. They would not do away with it for the world. Of course no sensible person would do away with private enterprise, particularly when we look around us and see that we have more production than this system knows what to do with. How can we blame industry for our present position?
What I have said shows the thinking of socialist members in the house. I have great respect for the hon. member for Cape Breton South, but only a few moments ago he said industry was supposed to take care of the unemployed, that it was supposed to give jobs, to guarantee annual wages, to give family allowances, and all the rest of it. I do not think any sensible person will contradict me when I say that the purpose of industry is to produce goods. In the operation of producing goods jobs are made automatically. It is the government's job through the financial system to provide markets, and one of the best markets we have is our market right here in Canada, among our own people. The higher we raise our standard of living, the more industry will produce to meet our requirements and the more jobs there will be. Social Credit has given the solution.
The hon. member says it is the responsibility of private enterprise to produce and that of government to supply the market.

The government has to supply the market, whether it be through foreign trade or in some other way by the application of their financial policies. Government policy must involve going out and finding markets for our exportable goods. Government policy will do this, in conjunction with private enterprise.
If that is not socialism, what is it?

This is done through control of the financial policy. The other day the hon. member for Acadia gave a good example of how the government could extend our markets by the acceptance of some of the soft currencies. It was not long ago that most hon. members voted against that suggestion. Through the manipulation of that financial policy the government could extend our markets, and through

the manipulation of the financial policy the government could make it possible for the people of this country to have sufficient purchasing power, whether through increased wages or salaries, increased family allowances, or national dividends, as we have suggested. I am not going to argue about national dividends at this time.
It is the responsibility of government to see to it that the people have the purchasing power to buy the goods industry is producing. When that falls down-as it has fallen down-the Minister of Labour finds himself in a helpless position. I am quite sure that if he were to ask treasury board for more money to take adequate care of the unemployed he would be told he could not have it. If I am wrong I stand to be corrected, but I do not think I am wrong. I would like to see the minister do that.
I said a moment ago that I was not going to speak as long as others have spoken. I may have exceeded my 15 minutes by a half minute or so, but I shall conclude by saying that during this session the minister has given sympathetic attention to the hearings in committees. I believe he is trying to do a good job, regardless of the handicap from which he suffers.
As the items are called I may have something further to say.
