Mr. Chairman, I would like to submit to the consideration of this house, on this occasion, a few remarks on a problem of interest to every Canadian citizen, that of the difficult position of our older workers in the labour market of this country.
During the past few years, recurring periods of seasonal unemployment have made all the more evident the difficulties and worries experienced by this very important part of our working force.
The plight of our older workers is not something peculiar to this country, but economic and social considerations would lead us to think that labour and employment conditions in their case will grow worse unless remedial measures are taken, and taken soon.
We all know that the population of this country is gradually increasing. Every year the Canadian nation as a whole is also growing more mature, and the number of our people who are over 45 years of age is daily growing larger. At the same time the proportion of young people under 20 is growing less.
Supply-Labour
In 1881 the number of Canadians over 40 years of age made up 20 per cent of the population of this country. Now this same group makes up practically 33 per cent of the same population.
At the turn of the century, there were 15 adults under 65 for every person aged 65 and over, whereas now there are only 7 adults under 65 for every person aged 65 and over.
In a survey conducted by the Department of Labour, which I have completed with other statistics, it is shown that the population of Ontario, which, allowing for certain adjustments, is fairly indicative of the general composition of the population of the whole country, was made up in 1881 of 16 per cent aged 45 and more, 38 per cent being under 20.
In 1951 this same population was made up of 31 per cent aged 45 and above, only 24 per cent being under 20. A survey of trends observed throughout the development of the Canadian nation over the past fifty years shows that, by 1971, 38 per cent of the population will be made up of people over 45 and that those under 20 will represent 17-8 per cent.
In other words, then, the increase in population and maturity in Canada is accompanied by a marked increase in the number of workers over 40.
But as the older element of the population increases another trend becomes increasingly noticeable. Casual observation reveals that employers of labour show a marked preference for workers under 40. That trend creates a feeling of insecurity, among older workers, all the more so in the wake of revolutionary changes which have occurred in our economy as a result of advanced and accelerated technology and the resultant acute competition in both our domestic and export markets.
Statistics issued by the unemployment insurance commission show fairly well how hard it is for older men to find jobs. For instance, in 1952, 36-5 per cent of the total applications for work received by the commission offices, everywhere in Canada, were from people over 45. The curious fact that this percentage remains practically constant throughout the year shows what restrictions exist for older workers with respect to job opportunities.
In the light of those figures, a fact stands out: not only must careful consideration be given to ways and means of helping older workers but, at the same time, employers themselves should seek to solve that national problem.

Supply-Labour
Many reasons have been given-most of them based on preconceived ideas-to explain the limits imposed upon the employment of older workers and the increasing difficulty with which they can share in the production of our national wealth.
In certain quarters it is said that this change which industry has undergone following extreme mechanization and application of the mass production principle has led employers to believe that older workers were slower in adjusting themselves to the new techniques and that accidents and absenteeism were more frequent among these older workers.
In this mad productivity race we have even been led to believe that older workers were slowing down production.
On the other hand, many industries have training plans which involve quite a large investment, and they have the preconceived idea that it would not be profitable to let older workers train for a job they would hold for a limited time.
Elsewhere, these same workers who are looking for work are handicapped on account of pension plans already in operation in many industries. It is claimed that to employ these older workers would make such pension plans more costly.
But, I think that the greatest wrong inflicted on our older workers is to be found in the common saying that the general public prefer and seek younger workers.
It would take too long, Mr. Chairman, to analyse both sides of the arguments I have just mentioned.
However, I think everybody will agree that during the second world war, when we had to call upon all the resources of our nation, the Canadian worker, whatever his age, did the job well, to the benefit of our Canadian nation.
Mr. A. R. Mosher, in a statement made in 1952, gave a brilliant account of the very important part which our older workers have played and of the valuable contribution they have made to victory. I would like to read that statement into Hansard. I quote:
Nobody will suggest for one moment that a worker whose faculties are weakened by age or other circumstances has a right to a job which he cannot fill efficiently. On the other hand, in each plant there are numerous jobs which do not require the same deftness of hand or eye as would be expected of a young worker. During the war, when we sought the services of everyone who could be useful, with or without training, we found that older people could make a valuable contribu-

tion to our war effort. They were more stable and more responsible; their attendance record was excellent and they were capable of doing quite satisfactorily the work entrusted to them.
Sure, the work given older people had to be of a particular kind and they were not asked to do work requiring too much skill, unless they could prove by tests that they were capable of doing that work.
It has been clearly shown that older workers have a great ability to adjust themselves to a new trade and that they derive much pride and satisfaction from doing their work because their capacity is recognized.
Moreover, it is to be noted that although industry and governments have set the retirement age at 65, many people who work for themselves, such as merchants, wholesalers and garage owners are still able to earn their living and manage their own business even to the age of 80.
That applies equally well to farmers who, generally speaking, can still look after their farms at a ripe old age.
A change of attitude towards older workers is essential. I sincerely believe that if an older worker still wishes to contribute to the nation's productive capacity, he should be permitted to do so.
Mr. Chairman, so far governments have done much to improve labour conditions. They have passed legislation on minimum wages, workmen's compensation, unemployment insurance, retirement benefits in the industry and limitation of working hours. Nevertheless, the situation of the older workers has become a very important problem. Unless steps are taken to help older workers, especially if the industry persists in allowing the increased discrimination which is being shown against such a large proportion of our manpower, the present standards of our welfare legislation will soon have to be changed in order to ensure to those Canadians the security to which they are entitled.
The ever-depressing effects on the older men with dependents of a lack of work and security not only affects his own family but becomes a threat to the welfare of the people.
Canadians who are having serious difficulties in finding employment are now resorting to palliative measures of relief, such as unemployment insurance or a pension system which only partly meets their family needs.
At the rate at which our population is now increasing, we may expect requests for very drastic social legislation, if the labour market for older men keeps on shrinking, compelling those over 50 to cope with more or less protracted periods of unemployment or to give up their employment altogether when they reach the age of 60 or so. As a matter of fact, I can see the day, Mr. Chairman, when the government might be forced to alter the

present scale of old age pension as a result of those conditions.
It is estimated that in 1961 there will be in Canada 689,300 people 70 years old or more in receipt of old age pension at a total cost of $417 million. And as this pension could possibly become payable at age 80, if working conditions of our older workers are allowed to remain as they are today it will then cost the state close to a billion dollars to support legislation of that kind.
Of course, the additional burden of this increase will have to be paid by people in the lower age group, who will also continue to assume all other costs of government administration. If this assumption is pursued a little further, we might even come to the point where all Canadians between 20 and 45 would have to carry the whole burden of our national economy. Our way of life could certainly not stand up to such conditions. The problem of older workers therefore needs the urgent attention not only of the governments but of the people themselves.
Several means were suggested in order to prevent such a situation, but I do not think it could be altered from one day to the next.
Can the guaranteed annual wage improve the position of the older worker by ensuring him either a definite income or a secure period of employment?
Could it be said that a more satisfactory birthrate might, one day, establish a better balance between the various age groups of our people? I dare hope so, Mr. Chairman.
At all events, I would like to submit to this house the opportunity of introducing in this country a national contributory pension plan where payment of a pension would solely be based on the age factor. To my mind, adoption of such a proposal would help the older worker overcome the feeling of insecurity which is becoming his lot, in view of a reluctant labour market with regard to employment possibilities.
A number of firms already have pension plans for their employees and the Department of Labour is associated with many of these programs. Any experience acquired by industry and government in the operation of these plans could serve as a basis for the study of a universal industrial pension plan. This pension plan should be flexible enough to allow an employee to transfer to another job while keeping his pension rights.
Supply-Labour
A measure of that kind has already been adopted in England following the Beveridge report and Canada should explore this new avenue of social security in order to avoid the disastrous consequences which may arise from the situation of older workers.
It is not the only means available to remedy this situation fully. But I am convinced that a study of such a pension scheme will give us an opportunity to work out an over-all plan which will include our whole employment policy regarding industry.

Mr. Chairman, I propose to deal particularly with the requests which have been made on earlier occasions, and which were repeated today by the hon. member for Hamilton West, that there be a general review of the labour relations act and labour legislation generally. This has been under discussion now for five years; it may have been under discussion before, but it came particularly into focus in 1950 at the time of the railway strike when a bill was introduced in this house during the emergency session to deal with the situation resulting from that strike.
It will be recalled that at that time we proposed a method by which the emergency could have been dealt with and the rail services put into immediate operation without introducing the principle of compulsory arbitration. At that time we emphasized, as we have on subsequent occasions, the need for recognizing that the situation which then became a national emergency was one that called for careful examination with a view to the solution of similar difficulties in the future, that departure from the established practice not being an acceptable precedent.
Five years have passed. As the hon. member for Hamilton West pointed out this afternoon, we have had vague assurances from time to time that the labour legislation is under review. We have not seen any evidence of it; we have not been given any assurance that this is being given the consideration that it requires. Therefore this afternoon I propose to deal with this matter from the point of view of the inadequacy of the legislation as it is today and the new emphasis which has been placed upon the need for a thorough examination of labour legislation and appropriate changes which will bring our labour legislation up to date and make it an effective instrument for the exten-

Supply-Labour
sion of good will between the organized workers, management and those responsible for the enforcement of our laws.
At the time the emergency measure was before the house on August 30, 1950, at the conclusion of my remarks in which I had put forward an alternative which would have avoided the necessity of compulsory arbitration but nevertheless put the rail services into operation, I reviewed the situation and concluded with these remarks, as reported on page 31 of Hansard of August 30, 1950:
We are sometimes inclined to exaggerate the number of disputes. If there is a strike, naturally it is noticed by everyone. What is often ignored is the vastly greater number of friendly and cooperative solutions that are reached by the system of collective bargaining that has been worked out through long years of trial and error. In finding a solution for this problem, let us not create equally great problems for another day.
In a spirit of good will, and with a desire to bring into operation these vital arteries of the life of Canada as soon as possible, we can solve this problem in a way that will protect the rights of all our people, the rights of every part of our community, will continue the efficient operation of our great railways, and will be to the best advantage of the nation that we love.
Those remarks preceded subsequent requests that our labour legislation generally be reviewed under a procedure similar to that which had been found so satisfactory when the national war labour board was set up under the chairmanship of the Hon. C. P. McTague in 1943 with instructions to inquire into collective bargaining and related problems. Without seeking to rub salt in a wound that sometimes seems sensitive, may I point out that the very uncertain attitude of this government toward public inquiries is emphasized by the number of occasions on which public inquiries instituted by this government have proved satisfactory along with the number of occasions on which they have not.
Once again may I point out that the government has given the best possible evidence that public inquiries instituted under the Inquiries Act can be most beneficial. One outstanding example was the inquiry conducted by the board under the Hon. C. P. McTague because the report brought in as a result of that inquiry produced the labour regulations incorporated into P.C. 1003 passed on February 17, 1944, which undoubtedly had much to do with the splendid team work that has existed between management, labour and the agencies of government during these critical years.
That inquiry emphasized the fact that with the changing conditions there are of neces-

sity changing requirements, but that there are certain basic principles which do not change and which are fundamental to the strength of labour organization and peace within the whole community in relation to problems which affect our workers. The two principles which are the bedrock of good labour relations are union recognition and collective bargaining.
I have no intention of embarking on what might be regarded as a political speech in regard to this subject, but I cannot refrain from making comment about the extent to which the Liberal mythology has extended, even into this field. I was present at a dinner given by the Trades and Labour Congress as a farewell testimonial to that great representative of organized labour in this country, Percy Bengough, just a few months ago. On that occasion the Minister of Labour, for whom personally I have the highest regard as a result of our long association, made a speech which I can only hope was furnished to him from records out of this mythology. On that occasion I heard the minister tell about what purported to be the beginning of understandable labour relations in this country. According to that mythology everything that really was good began with the Liberal governments in this country. Mr. Chairman, the applause from the other side, which cannot be reported in Hansard but to which I should like to pay notice, merely indicates the extent to which this mythology has extended into the minds of the members opposite. Here is another occasion where it does indicate that perhaps members of parliament themselves might well do a little reading of their own history from time to time. If ever there was a fabricated mythology, it was the suggestion that recognition of the rights of unions and collective bargaining began with the Liberal governments in this century, and particularly with the Liberal government under Mr. Mackenzie King.
I have in my possession an attractive souvenir. It is a gold case presented on July 1, 1872, to Lady Macdonald. On that gold case are these words:
Presented by the International Working Men's Unions to Lady Macdonald as a testimonial of their respect for the wife of Canada's greatest statesman, July 1, 1872.
What was the reason why the international working men's unions-the word "unions" is in the plural-were giving this beautiful box to Lady Macdonald on that occasion? It was not merely a gracious gesture to the wife of the prime minister; it was in recognition of the fact that it was the government

of Sir John Macdonald that in 1871 introduced the legislation which gave unions recognition, the right of collective bargaining and the right to strike. At that time-

It was not worth listening to.

I always like to hear some
of these interjections. They are usually so illuminating as evidence of the extent to which Liberals themselves have been fooled by their own propaganda.

The hon. member now says
loud enough to be heard, "It is too bad they did not keep it up". It just shows that he has not read the elementary history of Canada, because they did keep it up and I could go on for some time through the record of subsequent legislation. He does not know, of course, that in 1890, following the conviction of certain Hamilton bricklayers who went on strike in 1888 because of a local situation there, a law was passed which protected the workmen from any prosecution for conspiracy in refusing to work with or for any employer or workmen. It would be well if the hon. member for Halifax would just go back and read a little history. Perhaps also he might go back and read something about what happened under Sir Robert Borden when in 1918 he dealt with these very problems and at that time laid down certain principles which have become established principles within our labour organizations in this country, and principles, I might say, that the Minister of Labour before his political conversion would have reason to remember.
These are things that have gone right on through the piece. Since the hon. member for Halifax exemplifies the extent to which the Liberal mythology has been swallowed by some of the hon. members opposite, may I remind him that a great milestone in labour legislation and in the rights of labour came with the treaty of Versailles and the incidental features of that treaty. The labour organization of the league of nations was provided for and through the general council of that organization draft conventions were established for setting up wage machinery, hours of work and days of rest and other matters of that kind. These conventions were signed for Canada by a Conservative prime minister, Sir Robert Borden. Then
Supply-Labour
the ratification of those conventions stood through the whole period of Liberal government from 1921 to 1930, and it was the Bennett government that ratified those conventions. So the hon. member for Halifax will find the record fairly clear as to the extent to which the Conservative party has continued its interest in matters of this kind.
I would also point out that, in so far as these rights are concerned, it would be helpful if we all dealt with this on the basis of the record; and, with the friendliest emphasis, may I suggest to the Minister of Labour that in future, when dealing with the rights of labour in collective bargaining and matters of that kind, perhaps the position of Sir John Macdonald should not be forgotten.
I was dealing only with the present century.

But I am afraid that the minister omitted to read out that reservation when he made his speech, because I was there. However, it is made, and we shall take it as an amendment that would have been very appropriate at the time. Mr. Chairman, the fact is that the wartime labour regulations that were adopted following the McTague report were a very satisfactory basis of labour legislation in this country. True, there were certain features which did not meet with unanimous approval, but on the whole they did find general approval.
May I recall one interesting incident in connection with the adoption or the passing of P. C. 1003 on February 17, 1944. As some of the hon. members know, I was in the Ontario legislature at that time and in the session of that spring we introduced legislation there which applied in toto P.C. 1003 to the industries in Ontario for the life of that order in council. I may say that, not only did Ontario adopt P.C. 1003; so did Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and British Columbia. Therefore over a large part of Canada there was uniform labour legislation by agreement, not by any arbitrary imposition of that legislation by this government, but by agreement and by the approval of the provinces of legislation which had come forward fully digested and carefully prepared as a result of this report that had been presented by Mr. Justice McTague. I should say, so that the record will be complete, that there were three members of that board; two signed a majority report and one signed a minority report which disagreed with the majority report in certain details.

Supply-Labour
Was Mr. J. L. Cohen one member?
Mr. J. L. Cohen.
And the third one?

Since the minister has mentioned it, I shall mention the other members. The majority report was presented by the Hon. Mr. Justice C. P. McTague and Mr. Leon Lalande. The minority report was signed by Mr. J. L. Cohen. That report followed a long and extensive inquiry during which the labour organizations, social organizations, individuals and organizations representing management, as well as individual representatives of management, had an opportunity to present their opinions and to discuss their views with the members of this board.
I have mentioned that today because I think we can all realize that the more generally certain basic principles become established, the more clearly will they become known to the public generally, and the more firmly will be built into our society that measure of continuing co-operation between management and labour and the representatives of all governments which will assure that type of industrial good will which should be the objective of every elected member of parliament and of the legislative bodies throughout this country.
This is not something in which those who have been engaged in the active ranks of organized labour alone have a direct interest. This is something in which every Canadian has an interest. The rights of organized labour, the recognition of unions, assured collective bargaining that is really free collective bargaining, as the basis of the advancement of relations within our industrial communities are things that are very much part and parcel of the good society we are trying to build. This is something which is just as much in the mind of one member as it is in that of another. In fact, it should be the desire of every member to see this type of legislation advanced to the highest degree in this country of ours.
It is with that thought in mind that I have risen to refer back to what happened in 1950 and to recall that the government resorted to compulsory arbitration at that time. I have emphasized the fact that on that occasion we pointed out to the government that this is an unsatisfactory principle that should not be adopted as a precedent. Since that time we have continued to urge another inquiry similar to that conducted in 1943 under the Hon. C. P. McTague.
I close these remarks with the earnest appeal to the government to end the shillyshallying with regard to our labour legislation.

We have continued to ask for a general revision of this legislation to bring it up to date in the interests of organized labour, management, our whole society and our economic strength which will depend so largely upon the good will and harmony which produces industrial efficiency and has a good deal to do with our ability to sell in the highly competitive markets of the world today.
Before concluding may I repeat my request, which I believe is a reasonable one. I ask for the appointment of a committee with the full powers of reference conferred upon the Hon. Mr. Justice McTague and his associates in 1943. I have no hesitation in saying that I would even hope that the government would again appoint Hon. C. P. McTague, who showed such great wisdom and judgment on that occasion. But whether it be Mr. McTague or someone else similarly qualified, with others representing management and labour and such others as the government may deem fit to sit upon such a board of inquiry and proceed as soon as possible to examine this whole situation, I ask that such a committee be again appointed.
The need for examination of our legislation and an up-to-date code which would appeal to all Canadians becomes more obvious as we see this great association of two major labour congresses in Canada which will bring together a large part of organized labour in this country. It will be to their advantage, and it will be to the advantage of management which has such a great responsibility not only for the welfare of organized labour but also for the strength of our trade, internal and external. It would be to the advantage of the whole economy if at this time we now could have a comprehensive review and report by a committee which would examine the whole subject and make recommendations upon which up-to-date, modern and progressive legislation could be introduced into this house at the next session of parliament.

Mr. Chairman, I have just a brief word to say. I have listened attentively to the statement made by the Minister of Labour. I do not think it is fair for anybody to suggest that that statement was shillyshallying. It shows splendid co-operation between the minister and all his workers and he paid his tribute to them.
Somebody said that there was not any bringing together of labour and management. I am going to give a concrete example in Fort William where the Minister of Labour, through his representative, brought labour and management together. In the strike of the elevator workers things were at a standstill when the Minister of Labour appointed

Mr. Taylor of Toronto, and it was not long until that strike was settled. I think this is a splendid example of how the Minister of Labour and his representatives can bring labour and management together.
I appreciated the suggestions made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South. He says some things that are good and some things that are maybe a bit better. But when he emphasized vocational training, as others have done, I think he was wise. He also said that perhaps the officials in the minister's office are not paid enough. I am going to speak of these two things.
With regard to vocational training, I have spoken before of the things that have been done in Fort William to help labour. This vocational training is something that is being practised in Fort William today. The board of education takes high school pupils out to the Canadian Car plant. They will take them down to the vessels and to the elevators. They will take them to the fire halls. Perhaps one of the last groups to place their case before the high school pupils was the engineers. It is a well known fact that today there are not enough engineers in Canada to fill the jobs available. Therefore the engineers took this opportunity of placing before the high school pupils this need. The high school pupils were taken to McKellar hospital to see the work that the doctors and the nurses are doing. They were told that there is a great demand for nurses. This is putting the thing into practice. What are the other cities of Canada doing to put across this vocational training program? I should like to know. I should like to hear somebody say what is being done. Do it first, even before you tell it.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South said that perhaps the officials were not paid enough. I know this is true. I know in our vocational training office in Fort William the employees are not paid a living wage. Perhaps I should not say that, but it is a fact. I know of the case of one young man with a wife and family. He ran into debt. There was not much hope for him, but he obtained some help some place. I do not think a young man should be obliged to work in any office without getting in that office at least the same pay as that received by those in the income tax office.
I have another matter I want to mention. In Fort William we now have a strike in progress at the Canadian Car plant. From reports in the papers, according to the mayor of Fort William attempts are being made to settle this thing as soon as possible. The minister of labour from Toronto is up there. I should like to see the Minister of Labour
Supply-Labour
called on for his assistance. If that is done, I am convinced that soon management and the union will come together and the strike will be settled. I just pay my tribute to the minister, not because I sit close to him but because I admire the way he does his work, without bluster or noise and not very much advertising.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
The Minister of Labour has had quite a number of suggestions laid before him this afternoon, Mr. Chairman. It is my purpose to underline some of these suggestions and to add to the list. There are, indeed, a good many problems that require his attention and his study and I hope that action by him will be the result of that attention and that study.
However, before I go into the list of items I want to lay before the minister in one way or another, I must confess that when the Leader of the Opposition made his speech this afternoon it prompted me to send to the library for a certain volume of Hansard and also brought back to my mind certain facts of history. The Leader of the Opposition twitted my hon. friends across the way about what he called Liberal mythology. I have some Liberal mythology here which I shall come to when I get through with the Leader of the Opposition.
First, I want to talk about history, and this is not mythology. I come from Winnipeg. When a Winnipegger hears a Tory talking about the great love of the Conservative party for labour, he remembers 1919. He remembers a certain telegram that a gentleman by the name of Arthur Meighen sent to Winnipeg suggesting that certain people should be deported and that the legislation would be introduced afterwards. The volume of Hansard for which I sent to the library contains a record of what went on in the House of Commons on June 6, 1919. Sir Robert Borden, presented today as the friend of labour, was prime minister. I find that on that day the House of Commons was discussing a bill which had to do with government purchasing methods. As a matter of fact, Sir Robert Borden was speaking. The statement he was in the midst of making was broken off on page 3211 of Hansard for June 6, 1919, with a dash, whereupon he said:
My colleague the Minister of Immigration tells me that there is a very important bill to which the attention of the house should be directed at once with a view to its being assented to this afternoon. I would therefore ask that this debate be adjourned to be resumed again this day, if the house will consent.
Motion agreed to and debate adjourned.
I ask hon. members who are interested in history, and interested in what has gone on in this house in days gone by to get this

Supply-Labour
volume and just look at the four pages 3211, 3212, 3213, and 3214 of Hansard for June 6, 1919. Most of us know, because we sometimes measure the number of pages it takes to record our own speeches, that it takes about seven or eight pages of Hansard to cover 40 minutes in this house. This means that a page of Hansard is equivalent to about 5 or six minutes. I am asking members to consider what happened under a Conservative government as it was reported on less than four pages of Hansard. Now, members can do their own arithmetic, but that looks like 20 minutes or so, although it might have taken a few minutes more in view of the trip to the other place that was included in that period of time.
Starting near the bottom of the second column of page 3211, the house proceeded to give first reading to a bill to amend the Immigration Act for the purpose of deporting certain people from Winnipeg. On that page and on the next two pages, you will find that the bill was given first reading, second reading, considered in committee of the whole and given third reading and passed. What was the next item? Did they go back to this other business they had interrupted? No, a message was delivered by Colonel Ernest J. Chambers, Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod, and the house went over to the Senate where royal assent was given to a batch of bills, including the bill that had been put through that day.
With consent?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Yes, the Liberals consented to it, and Mr. D. D. McKenzie was the Leader of the Opposition at the time.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: What did Mr. McKenzie say?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: He did not say very much.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: He did not say, "With consent"; the interjection was wholly unwarranted.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Does the Minister of National Health and Welfare know what Mr. McKenzie said? I think the minister should get this book and read it before he interjects.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I have read it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. McKenzie said:
I have no desire to obstruct the minister but would he say in what form this legislation comes before the house?
There was no attempt to hold back the bill. It took unanimous consent to go through these three readings all in one day. There was connivance apparently, so far as the Liberals were concerned. But surely it is apparent

that the real villain of the piece was the government of the day, the Conservative party, which put through that legislation in that fashion.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: My hon. friend has said that so far as the Liberals were concerned there was a certain amount of connivance. There is nothing in the record that justifies that observation.
You should have said that there is nothing in the record.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
The minister can speak for himself, but if an attempt were made while I was a member of the house to put through legislation of that kind, with all three readings in one day, and I did not object, I would take some measure of responsibility for it. Most members of this house know I certainly would object. My point is that when the Leader of the Opposition sets out to give the history of the Conservative party with respect to its attitude towards labour, I think he should include all the items and not overlook this one to which I have just referred. I might mention also the attitude that was taken by another Conservative government towards unemployed people during the period 1930-35.
I agree with the view expressed by the hon. member for Hamilton West and the Leader of the Opposition that there should be a review of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. I think the time has come for a further look at our labour legislation. But I suggest that Canadian labour is not going to be fooled by this interest in the academic side of the labour problem, particularly when spokesmen for the Tory party make two speeches this afternoon without making any reference to the really important issues that are of concern to labour today such as the guaranteed annual wage. If the Tory party wants to address itself to Canadian labour, I suggest it should deal less with the history of the past, less with academic matters, and should concern itself more with the issues that are of concern to the working people of this country today.
As I indicated when I rose to my feet, I wish to underline some of the problems which have already been laid on the minister's desk and I wish to urge that he give them very serious study. He has under him a number of boards and commissions and officials who are well qualified to help him with this study, well qualified to do some of it for him. In the final analysis any decisions as to policy would have to be taken by the minister in conjunction with his cabinet colleagues. But meantime I urge that he seek the advice of his

officials and the members of the various boards and commissions which come under his direction, in the hope that some real headway might be made in dealing with some of these problems.
As has been already indicated, one of the most serious problems on his desk is that of unemployment or, to put it in other words, the necessity of achieving full employment in this country. I agree with those who say that this is not a problem solely for the consideration of the Minister of Labour. It is a problem for the consideration of the entire cabinet. But it does seem to me that it is the particular job of the Minister of Labour to bring before the cabinet as a whole the urgent need for full employment; and it is also his job to bring to the cabinet suggestions as to ways and means by which full employment might be achieved.
One of the suggestions we have made from this corner a number of times was made again today by my colleague the hon. member for Cape Breton South, namely the institution of the guaranteed annual wage. We were interested in the valuable speech made on this question some weeks ago by a member on the government side of the house, the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll). His suggestion was that the time had definitely come when the Minister of Labour should make a very thorough study of this question with a view to making a start on the guaranteed annual wage in some sector of the Canadian economy at an early date.
Since this suggestion came from one of the members sitting behind the minister, I was disappointed that he did not see fit to deal with this question when introducing his estimates today. However in that regard he did no worse than the hon. member for Hamilton West or the Leader of the Opposition. I would remind all three of these hon. members that this has become a most important issue, so far as the workers in this country are concerned. I remind Liberals and all other members in the house that the idea is certainly growing in Canada-and it is right that it should-that workers have just as many rights as business, industry, capital and all the other factors that make up our economy.
I said I was going to go along with the Leader of the Opposition by making some references to Liberal lore. I have in my hand an interesting book which I shall identify in a moment or two, and from which I shall read a paragraph or two. A certain gentleman was making a speech in support of a certain resolution, and this was what he said:
Not only does the resolution recognize that the labour problem is a world problem; it recognizes
Supply-Labour
also that the labour problem is a human problem. The resolution is based on the assumption that human personality is more important than any considerations of property.
I could not agree more. But to say that human personality is important, and to leave it only as a matter of words, is not good enough. I go on with the quotation where, referring to the resolution, he said:
It is founded on the belief that ethical and human considerations ought to stand above considerations which are purely business or material. It is an expression of the belief that industry exists for the sake of humanity, not humanity for the sake of industry.
I am sure some hon. members will now know the author of these words, although they do not come from a certain book to which hon. members might think they could trace them. Rather I am quoting from a speech delivered at the last national Liberal convention but one-the convention held in Ottawa in 1919. This speech was made by Mr. Mackenzie King who, on that occasion, was proposing to the convention a resolution on labour and industry.
In support of the resolution he went on to ask some rhetorical questions as to what was in the minds of those who had come back from overseas; and in that connection he said this:
They have interpreted the unrest of the world today in words the workman himself is using; they are saying that "man does not live by bread alone", that while wages may be one thing, wages in themselves are not enough. It is not enough to have work one day and unemployment the next.
Mr. King said that in 1919. It is true today; in fact under today's conditions it is even more staggering a blow for people to have to go through periods of unemployment and insecurity, be they short or long.
Mr. King went on to say:
It is not enough to have work one day and unemployment the next; to have work at one time and then, when sick, to be helpless in the matter of meeting the great problems of invalidity, of dependence and the like, where these things arise through the organization of industry as it is, rather than through the fault of the workers themselves.
So taking the resolution as it is drafted, the purpose as I have said is to recognize that as between the different provinces and the dominion we must endeavour to co-operate in working out a new industrial order, whereby, for the multitudes of men and women who spend their lives in industry, there may be a greater measure of economic and social freedom, and a larger measure of social justice.
Mr. Chairman, our contention today is that those words uttered by Mr. King in 1919, and others like them, should be put into something real and concrete in the form of full employment and a guaranteed annual wage, together with some other points which I shall mention in a moment.

Supply-Labour
But since I have quoted from what Mr. King said when he was proposing the resolution on labour and industry at the last national Liberal convention, but one, I would invite hon. members to look at Mr. King's speech and at the resolution itself. The resolution is found at pages 204 and 205 of the book put out following the convention. It is a lengthy resolution, but I would note just in passing-and I call this to the attention of the Minister of Labour; and perhaps the hon. member for Hamilton West will be interested in it, too-that one of the points laid down in that resolution 36 years ago was the principle that men and women should receive equal remuneration for work of equal value.
How long ago was that?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Just 36 years ago; don't ask the Liberals to do anything in a rush. They don't do things overnight. This, of course, was also the same resolution in which it was proposed-and remember that this was under the heading of labour and industry, so that, as Mr. King put it, workers might enjoy a greater measure of economic and social freedom and a larger measure of social justice-this was the resolution which included such things as an adequate system of insurance against unemployment. Note that it refers not just to unemployment insurance, with capital letters, but to "insurance against unemployment". Mr. King was referring to insecurity from any conditions which were beyond the control of the workers themselves.
It also called for insurance against sickness, dependence in old age, and other disability. It called for old age pensions, widows' pensions, and maternity benefits which should be instituted by the federal government in conjunction with the governments of the several provinces. And so on, and so on. As I say, it is a lengthy resolution. But my point is that it was long ago laid down-and we believe that the Canadian people agree with it completely-that human personality should come ahead of considerations of property, and that it is the job of government, supposedly of the people, to plan our economy so that instead of unemployment and periods of sickness without income, instead of insecurity, there will be full employment and something of the order of a guaranteed annual wage.
I call upon the minister to give more active and more vigorous study to the question of full employment than in fact has yet been done. I call upon him before these estimates are passed to tell us what studies he has given to the question of the guaranteed annual wage.
Will the hon. member permit a question? I have followed his advice and sent for the volume of Hansard and I now wish to ask him a question regarding it, if he will permit me.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Certainly.

The hon. member did not recall to our minds the situation which existed in Winnipeg at that time, such as I think has never existed in this country before or since, when law and order were threatened in a way they have never been threatened before or since. The hon. member greatly emphasized the fact that legislation was passed in this house in short order. It was passed by responsible people. He will agree with that. I should like to read briefly the legislation that was passed-
What is the question?

-and ask the hon. member whether he agrees that this legislation, which was directed against what we now call communists, was justified or not in the circumstances. I shall read briefly from page 3212 of Hansard of 1919.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I have no objection to this so long as it does not come off my 40 minutes.

I read:
Section fifteen of the act to amend the Immigration Act passed at the present session of parliament is repealed, and the following is substituted therefor:
"41 (1) Every person who by word or act in Canada seeks to overthrow by force or violence the government of or constituted law and authority in the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland or of Canada, or of any of the provinces of Canada, or the government of any other of His Majesty's dominions, colonies, possessions or dependencies . . ."
And then, later on:
-or by word or act, creates or attempts to create any riot or public disorder in Canada, or who without lawful authority assumes any powers of government in Canada-
I just want to ask the hon. member whether, in view of the situation which existed, he considers that legislation which included words of that kind was unreasonable legislation at the time and whether he feels it necessary to be so critical of responsible men who, in the circumstances of the moment, and with the danger which faced them, thought it reasonable to pass legislation quickly at that time.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. For fear that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre should attempt to answer in as many words as the question was put, I would ask the committee whether they consider an extended discussion on what after all is an amendment

to the Immigration Act which was passed 36 years ago is strictly relevant at this time?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think I can answer both you and the hon. member for Greenwood at the same time. Although what was under discussion formally at that time was a bill to amend the Immigration Act, it was directed against certain labour leaders in the city of Winnipeg. Those labour leaders included persons like John Queen, William Ivens, A. A. Heaps, George Armstrong and J. S. Woodsworth, as well as others whose names stand high in the history of my city. So far as the question about responsible gentlemen is concerned, I stake my claim that this was irresponsible legislation on the fact that in due course these people were elected to responsible positions by the people of Winnipeg. History has given its verdict against what was done here on June 6, 1919.
I suggest to the hon. member for Greenwood that even if, which I do not admit, he could make a case for the legislation having any validity at all, surely his own respect for the rule of law and for parliamentary procedure cannot permit him to condone what was done on that occasion. Instructions were sent by wire to Winnipeg with the advice that legislation would be passed afterwards, and parliament overrode all its normal rules of procedure to put that legislation through both houses in one day.
The hon. member for Winnipeg South is asking a question that would take me off into another debate that you, Mr. Chairman, might not like. I suggest that he can pick up the debate on the Criminal Code of a year or two ago, and he will see where I dealt with this whole question much more fully than I should on this occasion.
Hon. members are aware that the reason I raised this very dark chapter in Canadian history was the incompleteness of the report on his party's attitude toward labour that was made by the leader of the Progressive Conservative party.
To get back to the list that I had when I started, I urge the Minister of Labour to give serious attention to two or three other matters which are of real concern to working people of this country. One of them relates in part to the Unemployment Insurance Act. Because it can be discussed under that act I shall mention it only very briefly here. He knows what it is because he heard the questions that I asked the delegates from both labour congresses at the committee meeting this morning. I feel very strongly that the time has come, and labour feels this way, too, that the Unemployment Insurance Act should be
Supply-Labour
amended so as to provide for unemployment insurance benefits to include what is sometimes known as a sickness benefit. If I may go back to Mr. King in 1919, it is just as serious to be unemployed and without income because of illness as it is to be without income because there is no job.
The minister heard the delegates from the labour congresses say this morning that labour would be willing to pay its share of the extra cost to provide that kind of coverage. I am awfully disappointed that the proposed amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act which are before us do not include an extension of this kind. I urge him to study this matter thoroughly and vigorously. If it means that he must have discussions with his colleague, the Minister of National Health and Welfare, I am sure that colleague is always available for discussion and for help and advice. He told me earlier today that he always boosts good causes. Here is one to which he can give a real boost. I dislike the statement that was quoted to us, but this is one that I know is correct, because I have heard it from the Prime Minister, namely that the Prime Minister has told at least one of the labour congresses that sickness benefits included in unemployment insurance might be regarded as a case of bringing in health insurance through the back door, and that could not be done without an amendment to the constitution.
I admit that a sickness benefit could be one aspect of health insurance. If so, and if a constitutional amendment is necessary for health insurance, then that argument has validity. But I would point out also that sickness benefits for workers under the Unemployment Insurance Act could be regarded as a form of unemployment insurance.
When the Liberals met in 1919 they did not talk about unemployment insurance; they talked about insurance against unemployment. Mr. King presented the resolution and said that so far as the workers were concerned loss of income because of illness is just as serious as loss of income from any other cause. I suggest that a constitutional amendment is not necessary to include sickness benefits in the Unemployment Insurance Act. It would be part of the Unemployment Insurance Act and would be a step forward in giving the type of coverage which I think all Canadians should have. Here is an opportunity for the Minister of Labour to give real leadership in connection with a very important social advance that is needed in this country.
Again I suggest that the minister study this matter with the officials of his department,

Supply-Labour
with the unemployment insurance commission and with all others who have material on it and I hope he will come up with something of this nature at the very earliest possible date.
I wish also to urge the minister to study the question of the mobility of pension rights. I think he is in a particularly strong position to study this question, for two reasons. First, he is the Minister of Labour and is concerned with collective agreements and all conditions involved in labour arrangements in this country. He is also the minister who has charge of the Government Annuities Act so that he has experience which could be brought to bear on this other question.
I need not go into it in detail as the minister knows from the discussions we have tried to precipitate in this house before just how we feel. Some of us feel that one of the things needed for labour at the present time is the right for a worker to move from one employment to another and carry with him his pension rights. Many a worker is frozen in his job even though he may be able to get a better one because he cannot afford to lose his pension rights. On the other hand many industries fail to take in employees over a certain age because of the pension rights problem.
I do not want the minister to say that this is exclusively a problem for the Minister of National Health and Welfare or the Minister of Finance. They should be involved in it also, but this is a problem which is on the desk of the minister. It is an extremely important one and I urge him to give it active consideration.

I know the hon. member would not want to leave a false impression by the statement he made today about the attitude of the different parties toward the emergency legislation at the time of the Winnipeg strike. I am rather surprised that the hon. member did not make reference to the speech made by the hon. member for Quebec South, who made one of the finest speeches of his career in defence of the Winnipeg strikers.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, despite your attempt to keep me away from the 1919 strike my friends on all sides seem to want to keep coming back to it. I am pleased to note their interest, and I have no objection to the interjection made by the hon. member for Vancouver South. It is good to know that there was one Liberal with a capital "L" who had a little small "1" liberalism in his soul at that time, and I believe that hon. gentleman, the member for Quebec South (Mr. Power), still has.

If I can get back again to my list I want to say a word about a question which did get mentioned by the hon. member for Hamilton West and by the Leader of the Opposition, namely the procedures involved in the event of a labour dispute. Those two hon. members referred to what happened in 1950, all of which is a matter of record and familiar to most of us. I do not intend to go into that, but I would remind the minister that on January 11 of this year, as recorded on page 64 of Hansard, I asked this question:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Labour. Has the minister been made aware of the concern felt by the railway workers of Canada over the loss of their right to strike? Is the government taking steps either to assure these workers that they still have that right or to establish a satisfactory alternative?
Perhaps I had better be fair to the minister and read his answer in full, which was as follows:
This question, I think, divides itself into two parts. In the first place the Minister of Labour has been made aware of the concern which would be felt by the non-operating unions of the railways in the event they were deprived of the right to strike. In the second place I am sure my hon. friend has noted that the general conference committee of the non-operating unions of the railways have been meeting in Montreal recently and are discussing questions directly related to the second part of his question. In due course the Minister of Labour would expect to be told about the conclusions reached at these discussions and I do not think that in the meantime the Minister of Labour should anticipate these reports.
That was on January 11; it is now May 19. I hope that during the discussion of these estimates the minister will bring us up to date on that question. It is a question about which I could speak at some length, but I am going to boil it down by reading a few sentences from the minutes of a railway union meeting held in Vancouver in the early part of this year. I do so because the sentences which I shall read express my own views and seem to me to deal most cogently with the matter. I would point out that these are the views of railway workers who might be inclined to be prejudiced to their side of the case and therefore hon. members should note the fairness and objectivity of this approach, particularly as indicated in the last sentence which I shall read. First of all, I note in these minutes this statement:
A lengthy and representative discussion in which all delegates participated was summarized by the chairman who pointed out that the glory of the English law was its predictability. Men and organizations could determine in advance whether a proposed activity was legal and within the law, or otherwise.
There then followed some discussion as to what happened in the matter of the strike

which almost broke out in 1954, but for the threat made by the Prime Minister, and then I read this:
For a government to stand idly by during a long and protracted period of negotiation and fruitless arbitration and then suddenly intervene with the purpose of changing the law in order to deny its protection to one side in a dispute is the ultimate in caprice and despotism, in no manner different from the unpredictability of the law in ancient and modern dictatorships. As a very learned Englishman once pointed out:	A despotic prime
minister and a rubber-stamp parliament do not add up to a democracy. Other countries when confronted with a similar situation still find it possible to intervene in the public interest-
Note that "still find it possible to intervene in the public interest''.
-without threatening the destruction of the freedoms of common people. They do so by taking over and administering a threatened and essential industry until the disputants themselves reach an accord.
I wanted to read those sentences because it seems to me that they do two things. They point out how strongly the railway workers feel about what happened in 1954 when they felt that their right to strike was taken away from them. The other thing that those sentences do is to point out that these same railway workers put forward at least one alternative suggestion. It is in that spirit that I lay this problem before the minister as I thought I did by my question on the orders of the day on January 11 of this year.
I feel most strongly that the right to strike must not be set aside unless some more satisfactory way of dealing with labour disputes can be found. Any other way would have to be satisfactory to all concerned. I call upon the minister to give more serious attention to this question and I ask him to deal with it during the course of the discussion on these estimates.
There were other matters on my list but I think I have given the minister enough for now. If he solves these problems, then I will give him the others.
Since it is about seven minutes to six, I wonder whether I can call it six o'clock. If not, I am prepared to carry on till six.

No.
