speechtext: There does not appear to be unanimous consent.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. The estimates of the labour department as presented here today and as they have been presented in past parliaments give members of this house an opportunity to bring to the
Supply-Labour
attention of the Minister of Labour certain things that they feel should be corrected and certain things that they feel should be injected into the labour code in order to improve the working conditions of the labouring force of this country. At this moment I should like to deviate from the severe criticism of the Minister of Labour and inject a pleasant tone by saying to him how much I have appreciated his co-operation on the many matters I have brought to his attention and the expeditiousness with which he dealt with those matters, entirely to my satisfaction and to the satisfaction of those who were very much concerned.
During the past year we have been faced with a great deal of unemployment in Canada, more so probably than in any other year for a number of years. I had the opportunity to express my viewpoints on that problem in Canada, and it is regrettable that the government did not see fit to endeavour to remedy that situation. As a result, unemployment has not decreased to any extent, but has increased. Certainly, if not throughout Canada generally, it has worsened in various parts of this country. I feel that the Department of Labour and this government should make strenuous efforts to alleviate the present condition of those who find themselves unemployed.
There is a particular subject that I should like to bring to the attention of the minister. I suggest that he ascertain whether his department can institute some laws to rectify a situation where management in certain instances in Canada, in requisitioning labour from the national employment offices, makes very stringent requests as to the type of employees it is willing to take on its payrolls. I feel that this stringent type of requisition discriminates against a great many of our people. In certain industries at the present time a person who is over 35 years of age cannot obtain a job. If he weighs less than 160 pounds, he is not wanted in that industry. If he is less than five feet 10J inches tall, he is not employed for that particular reason. Some of these requirements also apply to the female help in these particular industries; they must be at least five feet four inches tali in their stocking feet.
It is no fault of anyone that they happen to be born of short stature or that they are over 35 years of age. There are a great many Canadians who at the age of 55 are very capable workers and are able to perform their labours very satisfactorily; and they are of mature age, so that they probably carry out their duties in a more comprehensive manner. The weight requirement is one that seems to be very strongly urged, and I see no particular reason why a man weighing less

Supply-Labour
than 160 pounds is not able to do certain jobs. Nevertheless, it is a fact that industries are discriminating in some instances, because of their requirements in the categories of height, weight and stature.
If at all possible some labour law should be implemented whereby the provinces could model regulations after this law, in order to bring about a discontinuance of this type of discrimination. The result is that those who have established themselves in particular municipalities where this industry is functioning, and have purchased homes and raised families, find that they are unable to secure employment. Certainly they cannot dislocate themselves from their communities and families and go elsewhere looking for jobs. On the other hand, this type of industry is requisitioning labour from other parts of Canada, thereby creating a situation that is worsening the present problem of the municipalities in regard to the provision of homes and every other facility required. At the same time those people who are residents and already established in those municipalities cannot secure employment.
I notice that in the estimates there is a substantial decrease over the estimates of the previous year-over $3 million. Of course, the two main items are under unemployment insurance. I am quite satisfied with this decrease, as we have urged time and time again that spending should be cut, but I am a little worried about the decrease in vocational training, and I hope that every consideration has been given in regard to this decrease so that the work of that particularly worth-while department is not hampered in any way.
Six o'clock.
Mr. Chairman, I shall only take five more minutes.
Let him go ahead.

I also suggest to the Minister of Labour an amendment to the B.N.A. Act which will make the provisions of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act applicable in all provinces of Canada be considered and be instituted. As the leader of the official opposition has said this afternoon, our labour laws are antiquated. I feel that as soon as possible the government should consider the revision of all labour laws. This should be done in co-operation with management, labour unions, and the government, all of them sitting down and exchanging their ideas on what would be best for the working men and women of this country. The aim of the labour department should be one of providing steady work and steady pay all

the year round. Of course, the co-operation in this respect should come as a result of labour and management working together towards that end. But the important thing is that the government should institute economic policies which would ensure steady work and steady pay. I feel that the government should reconsider its economic policy with a view to stimulating industrial expansion and a reduction of cyclical unemployment. Everyone is satisfied that much of the recurring unemployment, which brings suffering and hardship to our people as well as substantial losses in production, is not all attributable to seasonal climatic factors. With this in mind I urge the government to take vigorous action to remedy the situation and to aid through scientific and financial means the development of new processes and new industries which will tend to maintain high levels of employment and production throughout the entire year.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Chairman, this item gives the opportunity for a reference to several matters of importance of this kind. The situation in which labour finds itself is one that is challenging to the imagination and one that demands the utmost courage in the administration of those things that require to be done in order to maintain employment. The degree to which Canadian labour is mobile today and to which our population in general is mobile is indicated by the statistics given recently by Gilbert Jackson and his associates, to the effect that 50 per cent of Canadians change their addresses between each ten-years' census, that 18 per cent move to another address within their province and that 9 per cent move to another province. Indeed, the vast magnitude of the problem is indicated by the fact that of the civilian labour force of 5J million persons 3-3 million dropped out of that labour force in 1954 and 3-4 million entered it. In other words, it is a changing scene in the field of labour relations.
This afternoon, as I listened to my friend the hon. member for Cape Breton South referring to the dangers of automation, I thought he but repeated the age-old fear that has always been with man since the beginnings of the industrial revolution; in each generation, as inventiveness makes possible a greater production through the medium of mechanization, man fears the

change for many people believe it brings about continuing and extensive unemployment.
In our own time we have had experience with the vast changes that have taken place in the production of plastics. As machinery has developed and national production has increased, further and more extensive fields of production have been opened and vistas of employment have resulted that could never have been anticipated otherwise. Indeed, in an examination made by the Brookings Institution some time ago, it was estimated that by the year 1980 the average weekly hours of work will be down to 30 but that the gross national production will have been increased during that period in the United States by some 65 per cent.
While each generation fears that mechanization will reduce employment, each generation in succession has found that while mechanization has expanded to a degree beyond the belief of anyone of even 50 years ago, nonetheless employment has been extending by the extending field of other production. I think it was Professor Wener of Harvard University who recently made the prediction-and he is an authority with a world-wide reputation-that by 1980 there will be few factories with 100 employees and less, and that by that time one person pushing a button will have taken the place of 100 employees in the present state of mechanization. On the other hand, he predicts that in the extending field, as man's standard of living under private enterprise expands, the extent of employment will be maintained at a reasonably high level.
I should like the minister to have dealt somewhat more extensively with the unemployment situation, even though it was dealt with recently at length. What are the figures today? What have been the results in the last three or four weeks? All of us know that there has been a reduction in the actual amount of unemployment but is that reduction not slower than it was last year and vastly slower than it was at the same period in 1953 and in 1952? What is our economic position? Are the departments of government operating each in a closed section peculiar to itself? I ask that question because some reference was made to it by my friend the hon. member for Hamilton West in what I thought was one of the best speeches that she has made, if not the best, since taking over the responsibility of speaking on behalf of this party on labour problems. She covered the situation thoroughly and dispassionately but with a realism that is often absent in
Supply-Labour
the discussion of a problem which permits of an emotional impulse such as does that of unemployment.
What about this advisory council on manpower? My hon. friend the minister was kind enough today to give me a list of the officers and members of this council. It is one that is made up of outstanding men and women. The joint chairmen are R. B. Bryce, secretary of the privy council, and A. H. Brown, deputy minister of labour. Labour is represented by Percy Bengough, formerly president of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada; Donald MacDonald, secretary treasurer of the Canadian Congress of Labour; Gerard Picard, Canadian and Catholic Confederation of Labour, and J. B. Ward, Railway Brotherhoods and joint legislation committee; the employers by outstanding industrialists such as Hugh A. Crombie, Philip Gruchy, William Mainwaring and Allen Ross; the women by representatives of the National Council of Women, Mrs. Allen Turner Bone and Mrs. Flora D. Jutras; the veterans by Colonel Baker of the National Council of Veterans Association and Mr. Kennedy of the dominion command of the Canadian Legion; industry by the president of the Canadian Industrial Preparedness Association, Mr. McRea; and the president of the Canadian Metal Mining Association, Mr. Fraser.
These people operate or were intended to operate in co-operation with the representatives of the departments of national defence, labour, agriculture and other departments of government in which manpower plays a large part. But at a time when unemployment is rising, why does this council not meet? What is it? Is it window dressing or decoration, outstanding names without the use of their ability and capacity? What is the explanation? At a time like this, when a council such as that with its vast experience should be utilized for the benefit of the Canadian people, why is it kept in cold storage? I should like the minister to answer that when he replies. What is the manpower situation in Canada? Surely, there must be some body that brings together the statistics on immigration, agriculture, the labour force and the like. Yet we have never been able to secure any authoritative statistics on the subject.
Even on the question of unemployment the government cannot agree with itself. One department says there are 630,000 unemployed up to April, and another department says 390,000. The minister has a revised version that does not even equal the lower figure of the two. Surely, there must be some body that would bring together in proper relationship the manpower situation in our country.

Supply-Labour
May I ask the hon. member a question? To what does he refer as the "revised version"?

I have never been able to get an exact figure from the minister. The figure he gave was much lower than the figures given by the unemployment division and by the bureau of statistics. Is the minister now prepared to give us what the revised version is?
I am prepared to say that I have never given any version lower than that of the dominion bureau of statistics figure.

In any event, the minister did not accept the higher figure that was given by one department of government. I have never heard from his lips an authoritative statement as to what the proper statistic was in reference to unemployment.
I should like to ask him this. Is it not a fact that his department has been looking into the question of a national registration for Canadians in order to determine the manpower of this country, and in order to determine the degree to which immigration either increases or decreases job opportunities, as is contended in certain circles? What happened to this national registration episode of a few months ago? Is it not a fact that the government had a plan at that time? Did the plan not actually go forward to the extent that the entire machinery for the registration of manpower was built up, including the printing of the necessary registration forms and certificates? What was the purpose? Does the government have any intention of proceeding with the plan which the officials of his department were engaged upon for so long in the preparatory work? Does the minister consider today that national registration is necessary in order to determine the degree to which manpower is available in industry, in agriculture and in general for the economic development of our country, as well as for defence production and the like? Will the minister place before the house and the country the general plan that his department had in mind in the preparation of this comprehensive system?
Is it because of the fact that this council recommended the national registration that it has not been used or its prestige drawn upon since November, 1953? These are questions that the Canadian people would like to have answered. Certainly, the degree to which chaos is present in labour matters in this country indicates that the Department of Labour lacks direction, lacks system and lacks, not authority but direction. I ask the minister when he replies to state what has been

done in this regard and what was the reason for the preparations for a national registration. Has it since been decided to discontinue the plan? When was that decision made and
why?
Having asked the minister that, I pass on to one particular field of unemployment that has aroused a great deal of ill feeling, and properly so, amongst Canadian National Railways employees in this country. To what degree does the Department of Labour co-operate with Canadian National Railways in order to assure that the men who find themselves out of work are offered alternative opportunities of jobs? Recently I was in Nova Scotia for that great event when the first train crossed the causeway and Canada became annexed to Cape Breton. As a result of this accomplishment, a considerable number of Canadian National Railways employees find themselves out of work. What is the plan, and what is the attitude to be? What is the degree to which the Department of Transport cooperates with the Department of Labour in connection with this very important problem? Certainly, so far as Canadian National Railways employees are concerned, they strongly resent being pushed around as they are today. They believe, and I think properly, that there have been too many men without actual railway experience promoted to high positions. This has caused deterioration in their morale, and that is understandable when they see promoted to high positions men whose experience in the railway world is either little or non-existent. I ask the minister: To what degree is there co-operation, or is each of these departments-transport, agriculture and defence production-a closed compartment operating on its own?
There is one means of providing many jobs across this country, a means which would require an attitude of co-operation between the Department of Transport and the Department of Labour, and I go to the province of Saskatchewan for a moment for an example. The same situation prevails in the maritimes today. The people find themselves in a position where, as a result of a lack of power, they are unable to have the industry to which they are entitled. This incontrovertible fact applies equally to the western provinces, particularly Saskatchewan.
During the days of the expansion of our defence facilities there was a tremendous centralization in the central provinces. Today as a result of the development of atomic energy we expect that by 1963 power can be produced for civil purposes by atomic energy at a price comparable to the present production by coal. Within the next 10 years there

is a possibility that atomic power will be produced at a price comparable to the cost of producing hydroelectric power today under the best circumstances. Is there any cooperation between departments of government to that end? With the resources in the maritime provinces, is there any reason why an atomic energy pilot plant to produce power for civil purposes should have been set up in the central provinces rather than in the maritimes or in western Canada?
One of the major responsibilities of government today in maintaining employment will be the degree of co-operation between those in charge of atomic energy and those in industry. What we have to do today, above everything else as I see it, is to decentralize our industry and to give to the have-not provinces the opportunity to have atomic energy for civil development, and thereby bring about an economic situation in Canada in the near future where atomic energy will be put in overalls for the benefit of the Canadian people. That is one thing, in the great over-all plan, which I believe should be evolved in order to ensure jobs and employment in all parts of the country.
Secondly, there is the question of discrimination in freight rates. That is a matter that is holding back employment in various parts of our country. While I do not have the latest figures before me, I do know that, strangely enough, in Saskatchewan, with a socialist government in power, we have there a higher degree of unemployment- or have had during the months of January, February and March-than in any other part of this country. And when my hon. friends of the C.C.F. tell me that only their hearts are moved for the man who works, I ask them to go to the province of Saskatchewan and see what has happened there on more than one occasion.
Put down the figures.

My hon. friend is
aroused. I say to him that I gave the figures only a few days ago and I do not like to offer repetitious argument by placing the same statistics on the record day after day. I gave them the other day. Once they are on Hansard, then they are on Hansard, and can be read. And if my hon. friend cares to look back to a time about three or four weeks ago he will find that I set out in detail the comparable figures from Saskatchewan.
Indeed, when I listen to my hon. friends assuming the garb of piety, I ask myself why was it that, in some of the government
Supply-Labour
industries operated in Saskatchewan by the government of that province, as soon as the profits went down and the losses rose the man who worked for the government was immediately put out of work and put on unemployment insurance, or arrived there ultimately.
Shame.

That is what happened there. I dislike mentioning this, but I think the record should be clear in that regard, that by whatever organization a business is operated, whether by a state or by private enterprise, it operates to maintain jobs only when there is a profit return. And there are no jobs in losses, no matter whether the operation is government owned or privately owned.
I mention Saskatchewan-and this example could apply to other parts of Canada -because we have vast pulp resources in northern Saskatchewan. A very large concern has been desirous of opening a pulp and paper mill in northern Saskatchewan capable of employing a very large number of men. Yet that pulp and paper mill finds itself in a position where it cannot do so. Power is available; the market is available; but the freight rates, discriminatory as they are, deny the opening of that industry.
In that connection I am going to make one or two quotations, because I have a suggestion to make to the minister in connection with the manpower council. These are the representations made to the Prince Albert chamber of commerce on this matter, and what is said here would be applicable to all parts of our country that are subject to the discrimination that freight rates schedules impose on those parts of the country that should be developed. The presentation I have here states that the Prince Albert chamber of commerce are . . .
. . . seriously concerned about the present stalemate in the negotiations for a freight rate schedule that would make the operation of such a plant economically feasible . . .
Establishment of a pulp and paper mill in the area would not only provide permanent employment for several hundred people but would provide additional employment for woods operations during the winter season, such employment coming at that season of the year when the unemployment peak in Saskatchewan is at its highest level.
Then it goes on to mention a matter in the minds of people generally across Canada, as we export employment in the form of our raw materials processed in another country and irreplaceable here. Then it goes on to say:
Canada has already attained the reputation of being an exporting nation of her raw materials rather than an exporter of the finished product. Many thousands of cords of pulpwood are exported

Supply-Labour
annually from Saskatchewan to mills in the United States because facilities for processing are not available in this province.
The same argument applies in the maritime provinces where exactly the same situation exists in the matter of freight rates. The brief continues:
We contend that a long range view of the whole matter must be taken into account.
It goes on to point out that the development of the natural resources in our country should be on an equal basis in all parts of the country.
Then there is this singular circumstance in regard to the freight rates schedule:
Another point that appears to us very inconsistent is that the freight rate-*
That is, the rate from Prince Albert.
-to Chicago is $16.56 per ton while Winnipeg, an intermediate point and approximately one-third of the total distance, is $26.40 per ton.
Now, the effect of that is simply this, that it is better, it is cheaper and it is more economical to ship Canadian pulp into the United States to be manufactured there. It is $10 a ton cheaper to do it that way than to ship it to Winnipeg, which is only one-third of the distance, as compared with the distance to the American market.
The brief continues:
Surely the railways cannot justify this variation on the basis of per mile haulage costs . . .
We are of the opinion therefore that the Canadian National Railways, as a national railway, should be prepared to assume a share of the risk and make its contribution in a venture that will contribute materially to the development of the country and the establishment of secondary industries to manufacture our products.
I ask the minister this: To what degree are there negotiations between his department and the Department of Transport to encourage production in Canada, fabrication in Canada and processing in Canada of resources such as these which, at the present time, are produced here, and shipped over to the United States which, as I said before, is a process of shipping employment to the United States at the expense of the Canadian workers?
I ask the minister this: Will he outline in general something of the comprehensive picture, something by way of a general plan that operates in the minds of the government today to meet this problem, one that is so serious to those who are unemployed and so serious to the future development of this country?
These are but one or two matters that I thought might be of some interest, and upon which the minister, with his wide knowledge of his department and of the plans that his department is making to meet this situation,

would be able to comment to the committee and to the country. These are some of the things that, in my opinion, deserve attention. I ask the minister these questions once more, and I ask them in order. Why has this manpower council been laid aside? What was the reason for the work done by the Department of Labour on a national registration plan? Is it intended to launch such a plan? If it is not, how much was spent on the proposition before the decision was made to discontinue any further consideration of national registration to meet the competing claims of industry, of defence production and of agriculture and all the other claims upon the manpower of our country?
Finally, to what degree is there a relationship between his department and that of the departments of agriculture, transport and the like, to the end that in a community of council employment may be secured for many who are unemployed today?

Supply-Labour
the time not arrived when we should consider this whole problem in the light of modern conditions and in the light of the atomic age into which we are entering? The hon. member for Prince Albert, who just preceded me, referred to what might happen in the immediate future with respect to atomic power. I am quite happy to go along with him and I hope sincerely that his predictions are correct.
But I do suggest that if suddenly overnight we were to develop atomic power for civilian use in the various cities, towns and communities across Canada, we would throw into a complete tailspin the economic development that has been brought about by the use of hydroelectric and other forms of power. I am sure that none of us would want to see that; I am sure that we are all desirous that this process be a progressive one and that we will be able to start in a small way and bring about this atomic development to the point where we can use it to its greatest extent for peaceful purposes across the length and breadth of our land.
When I last spoke on this matter of people being thrown into retirement because of age the Ottawa Journal quoted what I had said. I do not intend to quote my words in full, but I should like to refer briefly to that article, as follows:
"In my opinion, the sooner that wrong is rectified, in respect of these men and women, the better it will be for the people of Canada and for the service they receive from their civil servants; the better too will it be for the government that makes the necessary corrections."
After his address, Mr. MacDougall told the Journal that to bar men in the prime of life from the civil service on account of age was "rank discrimination against experience".
I reiterate that sentiment tonight. I do not intend to make any accusations, but following my previous remarks on this subject I had an official statement that one reason why men of 40 or 45 years of age could not be taken into federal employment was that it would be actuarially unsound to do so because of the pension plan. I was sceptical at that time about the pension scheme. I recognized of course that if a man or woman was brought into federal employment at 45 years of age naturally at 65 years of age he or she would not be able to draw as large a pension as would the person who had come in at 25 or 30 years of age. I had a confirmation of that from one who ought to know his statistics with respect to these things, because he has offices in many places in western Canada. The Vancouver Sun published an editorial on this subject on

April 21, 1955, under the heading "Pension Bogey Exposed". I quote:
The letter which The Sun reprinted Wednesday from the Seattle Post-Intelligencer-a wife's broken-hearted story of a husband "too old at 43" to get a job-told a story altogether too common in industry and business. And altogether too unnecessary.
One of Canada's leading actuaries and pension plan experts states that this sort of tragedy is unnecessary. He is William M. Mercer, head of William M. Mercer Ltd., Vancouver.
The stock excuse for turning away the over-40 applicant for a job-no matter how experienced he may be or how able-is "you are too old to fit into our company pension plan."
"But it is only an excuse," Mr. Mercer tells The Sun. "It's nonsense to say it. The real reason why employers and personnel managers are reluctant to take on middle-aged applicants for jobs is that they are usually married and have children. It's not so easy to fire such a man if he turns out a misfit, as it is to fire a young man."
I would hate, Mr. Chairman, to think that the reason there is completely defined, but I believe in all conscience that there is some reason for believing the statement made by Mr. Mercer. If by any chance any of us in this house who are today 40 or 45 or more were to be suddenly thrown upon the labour market, I am quite sure that under the present regulations a great number of us would be told precisely what the married man of 40 or 45 is now being told in the various personnel offices of industry throughout the length and breadth of Canada. To me that is a very unfortunate circumstance, for surely if a man is in his mid-forties, is married, has a family and is desirous of educating his children, it is unchristian-if I may use the word-that he should feel in his heart that, though he has had years of experience, because of the fact that he is a married man with a family, he is unable to gain employment in many of the industries throughout the length and breadth of Canada.
I do not think we can blame industry entirely. Of course, industry is the great hirer of men and women, and thank God that is the case; but it seems to me that we in this parliament and this government have some responsibility with respect to this very issue of which I speak. Maybe industry will not follow our example, if we set a good example, but if industry did not follow our example at least we would have the satisfaction of knowing that we set a good example for it to follow. That example would be set if the government made a study of this situation and were able to announce in the very near future that men and women of 40 or 45 when they apply for positions in the federal civil service would in future receive similar treatment to that given to men of lower ages today.

There is something that can be said over and above what I have already said with respect to men and women of that age. We all recognize that, as far as physical vitality is concerned, younger men and women have it all over us; there is no argument about that. On the other hand, we have to appreciate that experience is one of the great teachers, and the experience of men and women in various vocations in life has steadied them, matured them and, like Scotch whisky, has aged them all for the better. They are in a preferred position because of that experience and their desire to raise their families and educate them, whereas younger men and women have not yet reached complete maturity and stability in respect to the vocations that they are going to follow in the later days of their life. I wish to plead emphatically that the administration give this problem its earnest consideration now-not next year or the year after, but now. If they set a good example for industry and for mercantile establishments throughout the length and breadth of the country, and draw into service men of the categories of which I have spoken, I am quite sure that the results to the taxpayers of Canada will be most happy and most satisfying.
It might be slightly out of order, Mr. Chairman, but it will save time in further discussions if I conclude with another request that is of paramount importance in the area that I have the honour to represent in this house. It has to do with the Department of Labour. I believe that men and women who wish to save for a rainy day and are not fishing around to get on unemployment insurance after we have completely revised the act, men and women who have gone into semiretirement, can today procure up to $1,200 a year. It seems to me that for many of those people throughout Canada it would be a fine step if we amended the act so that those who were desirous of participating to a greater extent than they are now allowed to do under the law might be able to procure SI,800 per year instead of $1,200 per year.
The people in my riding are not all numbskulls by any manner of means, though some of you might think they are when they send me down here, but the fact remains that there are some deep thinkers there. I know at least a few hundred people to whom individually and collectively this is a very important matter. If it is important in the riding of Vancouver-Burrard, I am sure that it must be important in dozens, and even hundreds, of ridings throughout Canada. Again I would ask the government to take this suggestion under advisement so that if 50433-249

those people of whom I have spoken are desirous of investing in the future welfare of Canada to the extent of $1,800 in annuities per year, the government may make it possible for them to do so.
Many of those people in that range of which I have spoken are men and women who have saved for a rainy day and they believe in the future of Canada. They believe in the soundness of investment with respect to government annuities. When they hold that belief, I think it is our duty in this House of Commons to give them every opportunity to invest to the maximum according to their desire.
I was going to quote from an address delivered in the other house by the junior senator, Hon. Nancy Hodges, on the question "The challenge of present-day estimates of old age." I am not going to take further time of the committee in giving to you some of the points that she raised. However, to my hon. friends to my left I will say this. If they want further information on it, and do not want to look up Hansard, if they will apply to Liberal headquarters and get the Liberal Advocate of February 15, 1955, they will find the address there.
The problem of age in this era, the problem of men and women living much longer than they used to live, is one that must be given consideration. I think I am safe in saying that when I was in skirts, with long golden hair hanging down my back at four years of age, the average length of life in Canada at that time was 45 years. That was a long time ago. Now, with modern medicine and modern scientific development in drugs, physiotherapy and all the various other aspects that make it easier for men and women to live longer, we have come to a state where, according to the actuarial statistics of insurance companies, it is expected that men will reach not only the biblical three score and ten but three score and ten plus two. I believe the age expectancy is now 72.
I recall that, not more than a few days ago, a gentleman in the House of Commons with whom I was speaking was telling me about his father who had retired from the publishing business when he was less than 70 years of age. The publishing company were lavish in their praise of him and they presented him with a purse. The amount of coin that was in the purse was not divulged to me, but I do not suppose it was very heavy. But they said to him, "You have been a great employee of this paper and for the excellent service that you have rendered in the part of the country where this paper is located, we are going to give you

Supply-Labour
a life subscription to the paper." He was 68 years of age when he retired. He is now touring the Mediterranean at 83 or 84. When he reached the age of 72, his old paper wrote to him and said, "Your life expectancy has been reached and your life subscription is herewith cancelled."
That is the sort of thing that makes me feel strongly on the subject that I have discussed tonight. I conclude by hoping and even praying that the administration will not only give this matter serious consideration but that, having seriously considered it, they will forthwith take off their mitts and dig in order to bring about the things that I have been advocating.

Mr. Chairman, the question of unemployment has been thoroughly discussed in this chamber, and the views of this group are on the record. The question of unemployment insurance was discussed when the bill was under consideration, and that bill is now before the industrial relations committee. I am therefore not going to take the time of the committee to discuss those matters that have been so completely dealt with. However, for years I have been greatly interested in vocational training, particularly of the young and displaced employed persons who require it, in the rehabilitation of the disabled and in finding suitable employment for our older workers. I listened with a great deal of interest to what the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard has just said. I might say that I heartily support his plea on behalf of the older workers at this time.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South this afternoon dealt effectively and, in my opinion, fully with the question of vocational training. Like him, I regret to see this reduction of $200,000 in the estimate for that purpose. Like him, Mr. Chairman, I believe that, instead of reducing that estimate, under present circumstances in Canada there is every need to increase it.
While we have a serious unemployment situation, I have noticed from time to time in recent years that there is a growing shortage of skilled workers such as first-class carpenters, plumbers, decorators, painters and of artisans generally who have thoroughly learned their trades and are capable of undertaking the particular kind of work in which they are trained. Industry in this country, such as the construction industry and those engaged in housebuilding and other types of building, need increasing numbers of skilled persons if they are to carry on with the programs they have in mind. If we are going to use to advantage

the human resources that are available in Canada, we must extend greatly our vocational training program.
Personally, in this day and generation, 1 think it is a crime to allow the natural capacities of many Canadians to go undeveloped and unused just because we fail to provide the machinery to see that they get the necessary training, guidance, leadership and opportunities. I think it is an injustice particularly to our younger people who seek opportunities. I think we should do everything possible to provide those opportunities by means of a considerable expansion of our vocational training program. Such training is an advantage to the young persons or older persons concerned, and in the long run it is certainly an advantage to Canada and will pay good dividends. That is all I am going to say on that point because I do not want to take the time of the committee at this stage to deal at length with these questions that I want to mention because they are of concern to a number of my constituents and because I have been particularly interested in them for some years.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South also mentioned the great technological improvements that are coming about in all countries at this time. I think it is safe to say that technological advance is now developing at a furious rate, a tempo that was never conceived of prior to the last five years.
About six weeks ago I had the opportunity of having a discussion with a young man from Great Britain who was interested in labour problems and who had made a considerable study of them. He brought to my attention the studies that are being undertaken in Great Britain in this respect to meet the problem which it poses, even in a country where they give more attention to this question than we have in Canada so far. He gave me one illustration to show what planning can do in relation to a technological advance that displaces a large number of workers. He told me about the Lyons catering people-they are the people who have the tea shops all over Great Britain-who recently introduced one bookkeeping and cost accounting machine into their headquarters in London that was capable of doing in less than three hours the work that 250 clerks would do in a week. There was a tremendous displacement of personnel when they introduced this machine into their offices. For some months prior to putting the machine into operation the management of the company and the employees considered the whole problem, so that when the machine was

introduced every one of those 250 displaced clerks was re-employed in some other position.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I think that is an example that we could very well follow in this country on a larger scale. In my opinion the question of technological improvement has not been scientifically approached by government, by employers or by organized labour. It is not sufficient to get up and complain about the question in this house or in the country. It is a very complicated thing that requires a considerable amount of study, and a considerable amount of understanding of the problems of management and labour. It will require some technical advice and scientific information. I suggest that if we are going to meet this question of technological improvements successfully in the years to come, we have to set about doing something seriously now. I suggest to the minister that we should have some form of special committee established to deal with this problem of the displacement of workers as a result of technological improvements. This committee should be composed of the representatives of government, management and industry, representatives of the employees and possibly scientific or technical advisers, economists from the universities or other sources in this country.
It is a complicated question. It is not going to be solved overnight. I believe we have to give it very serious study. I am not acquainted from firsthand knowledge with the technological advances that are taking place in most industries in this country. I am, however, acquainted with the technological improvements that are taking place even in the operation of the small lumber companies in the interior of British Columbia. For 50 years these companies have been content to operate with the standard type of mill and one type of woods operation. They employed about the same number of people to produce 1,000 feet of logs or 1,000 feet of lumber. Technological improvements, even in some small industries employing not more than 10 men, have been necessary in order to produce lumber competitively.
I can think of one small mill now where within the last five years technological improvements have taken two men off the carriage, which is now automatically operated; three men have been taken off the pond where they serve the jack ladders; two or three men off the cutoff saws and edgers, and another dozen men have been displaced in the piling operations in the yards. All this has taken place in quite a small industry. So far as the woods operations are concerned, power saws, bulldozers, heavy trucks and 50433-249i
Supply-Labour
big equipment are today making it possible to produce the same amount with fewer men. A few years ago the production of 1,000 feet of logs per day per man, on the skidway and ready to roll into booms, was considered good. Today they are producing 3,000 feet of logs per day per man. These developments have taken place in a very small section of the industry which has not developed to anything like the same extent the larger industries have. It indicates the problem we are facing at this time. I do suggest to the minister it is a problem that should receive serious consideration, the problem of the displacement of labour as a result of technological improvements and advances.
I should like to say a few words with respect to the employment of older workers. As I said before, I fully support the remarks made by the previous speaker. This is a very serious problem. I know dozens of older workers, men with excellent experience and training in various trades who, because of their age, are at the present time unable to find employment. I know this is a difficult problem. I want to say that the officials of the national employment service in my constituency do everything they can to find employment for this type of person. I know the managers in Nelson and Trail make a point of visiting employers and doing everything they can to find employment for these people. In the smaller centres it is particularly difficult to find employment for these people who are so well able to earn their living and whose experience, as the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard said, is so valuable and who could make important contributions to the production of this country.
Here again I do not think the government, government departments, the civil service commission or employers have really done all that it is possible to do to solve the problem. In this respect the minister knows that on several occasions I have brought to his attention the fact that the civil service commission refuses to place applicants in various departments because of their age. Only last fall I brought to the minister's attention the case of a veteran, almost in the prime of life so far as physical condition was concerned, and with many years' experience in bookkeeping. He had been employed for six or seven years in the Department of Veterans Affairs, but had to leave when the department was subject to economy cuts. In this case the man is capable of making an excellent contribution but because of his age the civil service commission failed to recommend him for a position, although he passed with high marks and had excellent qualifications.

Supply-Labour
At this moment I want to say that I will have more to say about this when the civil service estimates come before the committee. I have come to the conclusion that the methods of the civil service commission are the methods of the horse and buggy days when today we should be using the methods that suit the tempo of today's activity. I think government departments have been reluctant to do all that is possible with respect to placing older people in the government service. I might say that I have heard about political patronage when it comes to the appointment of persons to the public service. I have not experienced much of that since I have been a member of this house. I have not seen much of it, but I have seen a good deal of what I would call departmental patronage. I have seen positions held vacant for five or six months. People who have been ready to step in, and were No. 1 on the list, have become fed up and disgusted, and got other jobs; and in those circumstances those whom the department wanted to have the jobs were placed in those positions. I bring this fact to the minister's attention.
I do not think we are doing enough by way of providing employment for our older citizens. There seems to be a certain prejudice against employing older persons in some sections of industry, and also on the part of individuals who employ labour. As I said before, studies have been made in Great Britain in connection with technological improvements and advances, and studies in connection with the employment of older workers. Studies have been made in the United States by various groups concerning the capacity of older workers to provide a satisfactory service.
A most interesting study was carried out last year by the University of Illinois. In this connection I would quote from the Ottawa Journal of March 19, 1955. This article is most informative, because it seems that some employers seem to be impressed with the view that only the younger people can deliver a full day's work. They overlook completely in many cases the value of experience and maturity of judgment. This article bearing the heading "Older Workers Serve Well", and with a Chicago dateline, states:
The Civil Service Assembly says a new study shows the older workers are as efficient or better than employees under 60.
The assembly cited a study made and evaluated by the University of Illinois, which rated a sampling of workers on over-all performance, absenteeism, dependability, work quality, output and ability to get along with others.
The university contacted supervisors in 20 companies who told what they thought of the competence of 1,025 workers in their 60's and JO'S.

In over-all performance, supervisors rated 16 per cent of the older workers as excellent, 32 per cent very good, 36 per cent good, 15 per cent fair and 1 per cent, poor.
The supervisors reported that 70 per cent were absent less often than younger workers, 23 per cent about the same and 7 per cent more often.
On dependability, 50 per cent were judged more dependable than younger employees, and 6 per cent less dependable.
Comparative percentages for work quality were 36 per cent better, 57 per cent about the same and 7 per cent poorer.
More than 75 per cent of the older workers had production records equal to or higher than those of younger workers.
Thirty-three per cent get along with others better than younger workers do, the study showed. Sixty per cent are on a par with younger employees in this standard and 7 per cent do not fare as well.
I think this study clearly indicates the capacity of these older people, on the whole, to perform satisfactory service. I do urge the minister's department to do more than has been done in the past, not only to aid the government in employing more applicants in this age group, but to obtain greater cooperation from industrial and individual employers so that these older people who are found more often in the smaller towns and cities will receive employment. In many cases they are not old enough to receive pensions. However, they are anxious to work; and I ask the government to do everything possible to give as many as possible of these people the opportunity to do the work they are anxious to do and who, in performing this work, would be self-supporting, in conformity with their personal wishes.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to speak for a moment or two regarding the construction of vocational schools, because today these schools are more essential than ever before. Today many of the students from academic schools go directly to the assembly lines in factories, and from their first day of employment receive very fair remuneration. In those trades that require training and skills this is not the case; so we have vocational schools filling a need in this country which cannot be filled in any other way.
With costs of education as they are today, many municipalities are unable to supply the new schools required in those communities. The program we had in the past, of making grants in conjunction with the provinces in which these schools were located, served as a source of encouragement to the municipalities and the provinces to build the schools required.
This evening I am asking the minister to do everything within his power to continue this very important work in connection with

the construction of vocational schools. Under the British North America Act the building of schools is the responsibility of the municipalities. However, I do not think the fathers of confederation ever realized just to what extent the cost of education of the children in this country would increase. I do not think they ever visualized that every child in this country of ours would have an opportunity to attend a high school or a university; but that is the situation we have today. Indeed, I think we have advanced far beyond the wildest hopes of the fathers of confederation; and in advancing that far the costs of education to be borne by the municipalities have increased to a point where they are unable to carry the load by themselves.
I would ask the minister to take a good look at the requirements in Canada in respect of the building of vocational schools; and I hope he will be able to tell me that the usual grants will be continued for another year.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, consideration of the estimates of the Department of Labour affords an opportunity, especially for those of us who have the honour of representing labour constituencies, of making known to the house our humble opinion, which is undoubtedly also the opinion of those we have the pleasure of representing, namely the working people.
On several occasions, the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) gave the house statistics from his department. He has often accused us of quoting exaggerated figures, especially as far as unemployment is concerned. I have often been personally accused of quoting figures which did not correspond with those of the Department of Labour. I must say, Mr. Chairman, that the statistics of the Department of Labour, now as always, do not give a true picture of the situation in Canada. These statistics are supplied to the department by the various offices of the unemployment insurance commission in Canada and deal only with people who are looking for employment or periodically draw unemployment insurance benefits. If the department would only care to consult the different labour unions throughout the country, it would find that the statistical data given to us and the public are equivalent to 20 per cent of the actual number of unemployed. If the poten-
Supply-Labour
tial of our manpower in Canada is around 5,300,000 workers, I do say and maintain that actually about 15 per cent of these workers are unemployed.
May I be permitted a suggestion, Mr. Chairman? What would prevent the department from setting up a committee which could be called an advisory committee and which would include, for instance, representatives from the labour unions, management associations, the Canadian manufacturers association, the Canadian retailers association and the various boards of trade. These public bodies might meet from time to time and, with the information they are able to get, give the department a true picture of employment in Canada. In this way, the government would have more reliable statistics; it would be acquainted with the general situation and we would not be irresponsibly accused of quoting exaggerated figures. Moreover, it would make the government realize that there exists at the present time in the country a most alarming situation to which the government can no longer remain indifferent.
Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member allow me a question?
Certainly.
Does not the hon. member know that an advisory committee such as the one he is now advocating is already in existence?
He does not know. He was in Florida when that committee was set up.

Mr. Chairman, it is very gratifying to be entrusted with the task of looking after the interests of our constituents but it is a pity to have to hear the nonsense coming from the members in the rear of the house who seem to represent their constituents only through their interjections, and their foolish and silly remarks.
We are stating facts!

The hon. member for
Charlevoix asked me if I knew that such a committee already exists. If there is one, the department never mentioned it to us, and it never published any report nor any statistics.
The advisory committee I just suggested would be very efficient and be of assistance both to the minister and to his department.

Supply-Labour
Coming back to unemployment, I was going to say when I was interrupted that the government evidently is relying upon the passage of time for a solution. Although the situation remains most alarming everywhere in the country, especially in the city of Quebec and in the riding I represent, in spite of the many representations I have made for nearly two years, both in the house and elsewhere, in spite of the requests made by the various public bodies of Quebec city, the government remains deaf and does nothing to solve this alarming and sad state of affairs.
With respect to Quebec city most particularly, as I said, nothing is being done, no plan is being made. The Prime Minister, who, however, represents a riding included in the very city of Quebec, where such a great number of unemployed can be found, does not seem to be moved by the poverty which is rife, and is not even thinking of putting into effect any program of sufficient importance to cope with the situation. And what is more, hundreds of workers who during the war and since then had been employed in different arsenals, especially those of Valcartier and Quebec, have been laid off since January, which, of course, has not helped a situation that was already critical.
I know that when I inquired about that from the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Dickey), I was told that there were no contracts. That may be so. Let us hope that we will have no contracts and that another war will not claim once again the pick of our youth.
But, why not, for instance, turn these wartime industries into peacetime industries? If we were able to find money to make ammunition for war purposes, we should be able to find some now to prevent our people from dying from starvation and to safeguard in particular our human resources. So much could be done in these industries which, little by little, become empty, as unemployment increases, plunging our families into poverty and threatening to dislocate completely our local economy in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, this does not agree with the numerous promises we have heard made during the last general election, when the Liberal spokesman, with the Prime Minister taking the lead, were promising employment to all Canadians.
The Prime Minister even went around the world in a gesture of friendship and good will.

Nobody blamed him for it, but one day during his journey he met a large group of Canadian soldiers and told them that they would soon have the privilege to return to their country where they would find enough employment to ensure their own livelihood and that of their families. However, what happened? Many veterans came back here either from Europe or Korea, and now we see a good many of these poor men, who risked their lives for their country, gave their best years and sacrificed themselves, still waiting for their reward. They lead an aimless life, not knowing what to do, and the government, which had promised them heaven on earth, has not yet awarded them the promised subsistence, well deserved though it was.
There has been talk of a dominion-provincial conference in the fall, where this delicate problem would apparently be discussed. But, meantime, what are the thousands of people going to do who have nothing to eat and are living on public welfare funds, that can no longer stand the strain?
Yet, Mr. Chairman, projects are not lacking, particularly in the city of Quebec. I have mentioned two of these projects in particular in the two years I have had the privilege to sit here. I spoke about the reclamation of the Lairet river and urged the deepening of the St. Charles river. These are two far-reaching projects which, no doubt, would provide work for hundreds of workers.
My proposals fell on deaf ears. Not only were my representations set aside but not the slightest regard was paid to the requests of the authorities of the city of Quebec, of the chamber of commerce of Quebec as well as a number of other similar important organizations.
Mr. Chairman, why should the implementation of these two projects be refused? Not on account of a lack of urgency; not because these two rivers are not, as I have said, a constant threat to public health; but I am now inclined to believe that this request is being rejected because it has been made again and again by a member of the opposition and because they want to play politics with us, even with the hardships of our own people.
However, in 1930, Mr. Chairman, a depression arose following a too long term of the Liberal party in office. This crisis was equally felt in the city of Quebec, but in order to help the unemployed, we carried

out a big enterprise at l'Anse au Foulon, which, at a certain time, employed at least 3,000 workers from my riding. This project was achieved under a Conservative government. I only wish that this example could be an inspiration for the Liberal party.
Mr. Chairman, we are told that the government took many steps to help the unemployed. In my opinion, unemployment insurance is only a palliative and a poultice for the cancer which is gnawing at our population.
A poultice is not meant for cancer.
I did not know that my hon. friend, the member for Nicolet-Yamaska (Mr. Boisvert), knew so much about medicine. I thought of him rather as a lawyer.
It is simply a matter of common sense.

However, I see that he is a member of the Liberal party. I merely wanted to tell him that the Liberal party has never resorted to anything but poultices and it is still the case.
Mr. Chairman, public works are advocated. Such undertakings can only bring temporary relief under conditions such as we are now going through, but they have become necessary owing to the serious condition in which the workers of Quebec city now find themselves and which is a source of hardship for our working people's families who do not have enough for their maintenance.
The working people are not the only ones to complain. Merchants are also complaining and making efforts and sacrifices which I would say go beyond human capacity in order to avoid bankruptcy. Those that deal in the necessities of life are at this time carrying a greater amount of credit than they can really afford to. But those who are a little better off, with that kindness of heart which is characteristic of our people, as everybody knows, have taken over the government's job and have been feeding the hungry. I have already said so and I repeat it now. Unemployment is entirely a matter for the federal government who should be courageous enough to face up to the facts. As I was saying the other day, this is no time for palavers, for conferences. We must help those who are suffering, those who need help. That is the government's duty.
Supply-Labour
Mr. Chairman, when one looks at the government's actions, one wonders, sometimes, what logic there is in them. I have already praised here our part in the Colombo plan. Once more I express the hope that this plan will continue and be augmented as much as possible. What exactly is its purpose? To provide employment through large scale undertakings carried out in India, Pakistan or other Asian countries.
The lack of logic in all this is abundantly clear. Millions are given to various Asian countries in order to give employment to people who live thousands and thousands of miles away. And yet, nothing is found to give to Canadians. Not only are no jobs created, but those that existed have already been done away with. Such has been the case of Quebec city arsenals.
With regard to my own district I have already given the reasons why unemployment is worse in Quebec than elsewhere. I would like though to say that there is another reason, one which is possibly more important than any which I have already indicated.
Unemployment in this country is, in my opinion, due to the sharp competition of goods brought into this country from various foreign parts, particularly from countries with a living standard far lower than ours.
I am no political economist, but the least observant mind, the man in the street, could tell us that when it is possible to buy in Canada imported goods twice as cheap as we can produce them ourselves, we are facing unfavourable competitive conditions which are gradually stifling our industry and thus creating unemployment.
I think it is the duty of the government to take drastic but necessary measures in order to protect our industries, and especially our labour market, in such fields as textiles, electrical appliances, footwear, rubber goods, etc.
In the city of Quebec the basic industry has been for a number of years the footwear industry. Now in 1954 it seems that, on the basis of information available to me, we imported from England almost 2 million pairs of shoes, while several of our manufacturers in the city and district of Quebec were compelled either to close down or, in the case of those who could stand the competition, to stay open only two or three days a week.
How can we meet competition and create employment when certain products, which are now coming from Hong Kong, are sell-

Supply-Labour
ing on the Canadian market for $1.05 less than they cost us to produce?
For instance, shoe merchants are now importing from Hong Kong running-shoes that children and sportsmen wear in the summer time at the price of 90 cents. On the other hand, the Canadian rubber industry, which is one of the most important and gives employment to a great many people, on account of our living standard, which is, as we all know, superior to the living standard in Hong Kong, cannot produce a shoe of similar quality and sell it for less than $1.95 to retailers. It can therefore be said that, while selling both products for the same amount, the retailer prefers to buy the goods cheaper, even if he has to buy them abroad.
This, to my mind, is unfair competition, because the Canadian people cannot be asked to reduce their living standard to such an extent as to equal that of Hong Kong and other Asiatic countries.
The other day, I heard this somewhat surprising remark from the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe): "We must buy in order to sell." And I also heard the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) reply to this announcement as follows: "My mother always taught me that it was necessary to sell in order to buy." This is very logical, Mr. Chairman. If you have not the necessary money, you cannot buy. If you cannot buy, there will be stockpiling. If there is stockpiling, manufacturers cannot pile up more stocks from day to day, and there will necessarily be unemployment.
I therefore ask the government to undertake a very serious inquiry into this situation which is getting somewhat hopeless in certain parts of the country.
I ask the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) to speak on behalf of workers who are begging for work and are asking the government's assistance; I ask the minister to make his colleagues of the cabinet understand that the situation is serious and cannot be tolerated any longer, especially in Quebec city.
I know that the members of the cabinet are human beings and that when they have been acquainted with the deplorable situation prevailing in our district they will be bound to look for a solution. Under such circumstances, the solution does not lie in mere poultices, but in important steps that will bring about work first and then prosperity.
We hear about communism. As I stated the other day, communism, especially in Italy, was the result of misery and poverty. Here we fear communism and we have

reason to do so. We must fight communism and I believe one of the best ways of doing so is to feed all those who are hungry, by giving them work.
Canada is enormously rich and it is illogical to see some of our fellow citizens deprived of everything while near at hand there is abundant wealth.
Mr. Chairman, I repeat my request to the hon. minister. I know that he will take my remarks in good part and that he will strive to alleviate hardship in the homes of many of our fellow citizens.
Would the hon. member allow me a question?
Again?
As I am interested in the welfare of the unemployed, would the hon. member tell me how many people were without work in the city of Quebec on January 1, 1955, and how many there are now?

Mr. Chairman, it is a very interesting question to which I will most willingly reply. There were, on the 1st of January, 1955, in the city of Quebec, more than 20,000 unemployed and at present the number is about two or three thousand less. While some of those who were out of work at that time have been able to find jobs, either in construction or in some other industry, this decrease has been almost offset by all those whom the government has dismissed from the Valcartier and Quebec arsenals.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole

there was a question of privilege involved was, in my opinion, for the Chair to decide. It being ten o'clock, shall I report progress and ask leave to sit again?
Item stands.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, should the Department of Labour be completed tomorrow, we will go on with agriculture.

It being three minutes after ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
39S5
Friday, May 20, 1955
